# 關於 Think BIG

Think BIG（大想成業有限公司）是總部位於台灣、服務全球的企業 AI Agent 導入商。我們從守護企業資安出發，以 TB FRAME（我們的四階段導入方法：評估、建置、驗證、維運）把 AI Agent 建在公司自己的環境裡（公司設備，或公司名下的雲端主機），並提供一年陪跑維運。選地端版時，模型與文件都在公司設備內處理；選雲端輔助版時，問題與檢索到的文件段落會送到模型廠商處理。我們扮演企業的遠端 FDE（Forward Deployed Engineer，前沿部署工程師）團隊：從聽懂需求、建置知識庫與 AI Agent、上線，到後續維運，一手包辦；另有個人 AI 助理搭建方案。

地端部署不等於所有連線都在本機。若使用雲端模型或外部服務，相關請求仍會送出；需要資料不出公司時，須確認本機模型、外連限制與可用功能。

## 公司與服務範圍

Think BIG 的公司全名為大想成業有限公司，統一編號 62136066，總部位於台灣，服務範圍涵蓋全球。服務包含企業 AI Agent 導入、流程整合、資料與權限設計、情境驗收及年度治理與維運；另提供個人 AI 助理搭建與維護方案。

## 以 TB FRAME 管理交付

Assess 評估定義、Build 架構建置、Validate 驗證交付、Operate 治理維運，是導入方法的四個階段。TB READINESS（導入前自評，先確認流程、資料與準備條件）  提供初步自評；TB DELIVERY（依確認的範圍建置、測試並交付 AI 工作流程）  涵蓋導入建置；TB CONTINUITY（導入後一年的維護、問題追蹤與使用調整）  銜接年度治理與維運。企業服務依確認的範圍個別報價；三種方案於範圍凍結與資料到位後 30 天內交付。

[閱讀階段交付物與覆核責任](https://thinkbigtw.com/enterprise/process/)

依最小權限配置資料與操作範圍。對外發送、花費及正式系統異動由指定負責人核准，變更留下原因、範圍、復原方式與驗證紀錄。

# 雙 AI Agent | Think BIG!

個人 AI 助理

# 雙 AI Agent

單獨裝是兩個孤島，我們裝完是一個團隊。

OpenClaw（執行型）＋ Hermes（學習型）雙系統同機部署，並透過 MCP（Model Context Protocol）把兩者的記憶層與技能庫實際打通 ：一邊學到的東西，另一邊也知道。OpenClaw 第一天即戰力，Hermes 持續把成功經驗變成新技能——一套會越用越強的雙 AI 助理系統。

## 你是不是每天都在——

- 想要 AI「馬上能用」，又想要它「越用越聰明」，卻只能二選一？

- 裝了好幾個 AI 工具，各記各的、各做各的，彼此完全不通？

- 教會了 A 工具的事，換到 B 工具又要全部重教一次？

## 怎麼運行

1

收到 你從通訊軟體或協作會議室下指令

2

判斷 任務進到共享記憶層——OpenClaw 查「現在怎麼做最快」，Hermes 查「以前學過什麼」

3

執行 OpenClaw 出手執行；Hermes 把成功方法轉成新技能，寫回共享技能庫

4

回報 結果推播到你的通訊軟體；下次同類任務，兩邊都變快

支援再串接你的 coding agent（Claude Code／Codex 等），啟用跨 Agent 協作會議室。

## 你得到什麼

- 雙系統安裝部署＋ MCP 記憶互通（實際打通，非兩套各跑各的）

- 技能配置 OpenClaw＋Hermes 雙 AI Agent，技能數依訪談配置 （下單前先聊需求）

- Coding Agent 串接＋跨 Agent 協作會議室（串 2 個以上 Agent 時啟用）

- 一套持續進化的系統：今天的任務成果，變成明天的內建能力

- 2 小時線上技術導覽＋安裝後 7 天 技術諮詢

- 服務費依需求報價，無月費 （指我方服務費），請至[蝦皮賣場](https://shopee.tw/shop/105010395)選購

不想自己維護？→ [看「尊榮年約」](https://thinkbigtw.com/annual-pro/)或[「年度旗艦」](https://thinkbigtw.com/annual-flagship/)，全年有工程師陪跑。

方案價格

# What AI Agents Are There? Will New AI Agents Replace the Lobster? | 2026 Overview | Think BIG

[Home](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/) / [Guides](https://thinkbigtw.com/guides/) / AI Agents

AI Agent Overview · 2026

# Will New AI Agents Replace the Lobster (OpenClaw)?

Think BIG Editorial

Grok, Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and others are launching fast. This guide covers what AI Agents are available in 2026, how each charges for usage, what to do when quotas run out, and where OpenClaw fits for long-running tasks.

Last updated: 2026-10-02 | Data verified: 2026-09-30

New AI Agents will not make OpenClaw (the Lobster) obsolete — they are designed for different purposes. Each one is excellent. But for long-running tasks where cost control matters, brand AI Agents are not the first choice, though they are great for collaboration.

- Brand AI Agents tie costs to subscription quotas. They suit collaboration tasks within brand ecosystems (Gmail, Teams, WhatsApp).

- Open-source AI Agents (like OpenClaw, Hermes) let you choose your own model and pay per actual usage — suitable for 24/7 operations with predictable costs.

- The two types work well together: run OpenClaw for long-running routine tasks; use brand AI Agents for collaboration or ecosystem-specific work.

## Key Takeaway

Each one is excellent. But for long-running tasks where cost control matters, brand AI Agents are not the first choice — though they are great for collaboration.

## Common AI Agents in 2026

Data verified: 2026-09-30. Prices are from official brand websites. All prices shown in original currency; no self-calculated conversions. Labels: [Official] from brand website or blog; [Third-party] media only; [To verify] not disclosed by vendor.

### Two Main Types

- Brand AI Agents  — subscription-based, fixed monthly fee with usage quota. Examples: Claude, ChatGPT Agent, Gemini Spark, Grok Bot, Muse, Copilot Autopilot, Manus.

- Open-source AI Agents  — software is free; model usage fees paid directly to your chosen model provider, or use a local model for zero model fees. Examples: OpenClaw (Lobster), Hermes Agent.

### Claude (Anthropic)

- What it is : Anthropic's AI assistant, integrated background task completion (reports, research) since September 2026. [Official]

- How to use : Web, desktop app, mobile, Claude Code; all share one usage limit. [Official]

- Pricing : Free (limited); Pro and Max plans available — see [claude.com/pricing](https://claude.com/pricing). Usage limits reset on 5-hour and weekly cycles; paid plans can purchase usage credits. [Official]

- Available in Taiwan : Yes. [Official]

- Source : [claude.com/pricing](https://claude.com/pricing), verified 2026-09-30.

### ChatGPT Agent and dots (OpenAI)

- What it is : ChatGPT Agent uses a virtual browser to complete multi-step tasks; dots (launched 2026-09-29) is a 24/7 AI Agent with its own cloud computer, connected to 4,000+ apps. [Official]

- How to use : Select "agent" in ChatGPT tools or type /agent; dots is accessible via ChatGPT, Slack, and Teams. [Official]

- Pricing : Plus and Pro plans available — see [openai.com/chatgpt/pricing](https://openai.com/chatgpt/pricing/). ChatGPT Agent and Codex share the same agentic quota; dots is included in Pro and Business Premium. [Official]

- Available in Taiwan : ChatGPT Agent yes; dots availability [To verify]. [Official]

- Source : [ChatGPT agent help](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11752874-chatgpt-agent), [dots launch](https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/), verified 2026-09-30.

### Gemini Spark (Google)

- What it is : Google's 24/7 personal AI Agent that works in the background even when your device is off, connected to Gmail, Calendar, and Drive. [Official]

- How to use : Requires Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription; must be 18+ with a personal Google account. [Official]

- Pricing : AI Pro and AI Ultra plans available — see [gemini.google/subscriptions](https://gemini.google/subscriptions/). Usage calculated by computation, recovering every 5 hours up to a weekly cap. [Official]

- Available in Taiwan : Not on the exclusion list; actual availability [To verify].

- Source : [gemini.google/subscriptions](https://gemini.google/subscriptions/), verified 2026-09-30.

### Grok Bot (xAI)

- What it is : xAI's persistent AI teammate (launched August 2026) with its own cloud computer, browser and terminal; multiple can run simultaneously. [Official]

- How to use : Available on macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android. [Official]

- Pricing : SuperGrok and SuperGrok Plus plans — both include Grok Bot. All Grok products share one weekly usage pool; heavy video or long tasks consume more quota. Extra Usage Credits available (web only, 1-year validity) — see [x.ai/pricing](https://x.ai/pricing). [Official]

- Available in Taiwan : No official country list published [To verify]. [Official]

- Source : [x.ai/pricing](https://x.ai/pricing), verified 2026-09-30.

### Muse (Meta)

- What it is : Meta's personal AI Agent (launched 2026-09-08) running in a dedicated virtual machine; can browse, fill forms, send emails, and make bookings. Confirms before sending or paying. [Official]

- How to use : iOS, Android app and muse.ai. Currently limited to the US; Canada opened 2026-09-18. [Official]

- Pricing : Free (limited); Power (5B Muse tokens/week) and Maximum (30B Muse tokens/week) plans available — see [meta.com/ai/muse](https://www.meta.com/ai/muse/). [Official]

- Available in Taiwan : Not currently available. [Official]

- Source : [Meta Newsroom](https://about.fb.com/news/2026/09/introducing-muse-personal-ai-agent/), verified 2026-09-30.

### OpenClaw — the Lobster (Open-source)

- What it is : OpenClaw is an open-source personal AI assistant, often called "the Lobster" in Taiwan. Installed on your own computer; accessed via WhatsApp, Telegram or other chat apps. Supports both local and cloud models. [Official]

- How to use : Runs on Windows and macOS. Can be used standalone or paired with Hermes for a dual-agent setup.

- Pricing : Software is free. Model costs depend on your chosen provider and actual usage. [Official]

- Available in Taiwan : Yes (self-install). [Official]

- Source : OpenClaw official documentation, verified 2026-09-30. → [Installation guide (中)](https://thinkbigtw.com/guides/openclaw-daizhuang/)

## Two Approaches: How They Differ

The following compares approach types only — no rankings, no scores.

Dimension
Brand AI Agents
Open-source AI Agents (e.g. OpenClaw, Hermes)
Pricing Fixed monthly fee with usage quota included Pay per actual usage to your chosen model provider; software is free

When quota runs out Wait for reset, upgrade, or purchase credits No quota concept; costs scale with usage; budget-driven control

24/7 operation Varies by plan; some continue when your device is off Requires your computer to stay on (local install); or use cloud model API remotely

Model flexibility Usually locked to the brand's own model Choose any model: subscription plan, API, or local model

Data location Subject to brand's privacy policy; typically in brand cloud Local install — data stays on your computer; messages still sent to model provider when using cloud models

Best for Brand ecosystem collaboration (Gmail, Teams, WhatsApp); short high-intensity tasks Long-running 24/7 routines; scheduled tasks; cost-controlled operations

Each one is excellent. But for long-running tasks where cost control matters, brand AI Agents are not the first choice — though they are great for collaboration.

## What To Do When Your Quota Runs Out

- Claude (Anthropic) : 5-hour segment limit plus weekly cap; paid plans can purchase usage credits. (Source: [official](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11647753-how-do-usage-and-length-limits-work), verified 2026-09-30)

- ChatGPT Agent (OpenAI) : Monthly limit per plan; credits available for purchase. (Source: [official](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12642688), verified 2026-09-30)

- Grok Bot (xAI) : Weekly pool resets; Extra Usage Credits available for purchase (web only). (Source: [official](https://docs.x.ai/grok/faq), verified 2026-09-30)

- Gemini Spark (Google) : Computation-based, recovers every 5 hours up to weekly cap; Pro/Ultra can purchase AI credits. (Source: [official](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/google-one/google-ai-subscriptions/), verified 2026-09-30)

- Muse (Meta) : Upgrade or wait for free quota to recover. Power: 5B tokens/week; Maximum: 30B tokens/week. (Source: [official](https://www.meta.com/help/subscriptions/1021145227643680/), verified 2026-09-30)

General approach: route long-running background work to an open-source AI Agent (like OpenClaw, Hermes) — use brand AI Agents for collaboration tasks when needed. → [OpenClaw + coding agent collaboration](https://thinkbigtw.com/full-agent/)

## Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Will new AI Agents replace OpenClaw (the Lobster)?

The two serve different purposes and work well together. Common brand AI Agents in 2026 include Grok Bot (xAI), Claude (Anthropic), ChatGPT Agent and dots (OpenAI), Gemini Spark (Google), Muse (Meta), Copilot Autopilot (Microsoft), and Manus. Each one is excellent, but for long-running tasks where cost control matters, brand AI Agents are not the first choice — though they are great for collaboration. OpenClaw and Hermes, as open-source AI Agents, let you choose your own model, pay per actual usage, and run 24/7.

Q: What AI Agents are available in 2026?

Two main types: (1) Brand AI Agents — subscription-based with usage quotas, such as Claude, ChatGPT Agent, Gemini Spark, Grok Bot, Muse, Copilot Autopilot, Manus. (2) Open-source AI Agents — software is free, you pay per model usage, such as OpenClaw (Lobster) and Hermes Agent.

Q: What should I do when my AI subscription quota runs out?

Common options: wait for quota reset, upgrade your plan, purchase additional credits, or route long-running background work to an open-source AI Agent (like OpenClaw) that charges per actual usage.

Q: Can brand AI Agents and OpenClaw be used together?

Yes. A common setup: OpenClaw handles 24/7 routine tasks; brand AI Agents handle collaboration tasks or ecosystem-specific work. → [OpenClaw + coding agent](https://thinkbigtw.com/full-agent/) / [Dual AI Agent plan](https://thinkbigtw.com/dual-agent/)

Q: Does Think BIG's pricing include AI model fees?

No. Think BIG's service fee covers installation and setup only. Third-party AI model usage fees are calculated based on your actual usage and paid directly to the model provider. See [FAQ](https://thinkbigtw.com/faq/).

# Rolled Out AI and Nobody Uses It? The Problem Usually Isn't the AI. Work Backward From the One Task Employees Actually Do Every Day | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Field Notes · Issue 009
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

AI DEPLOYMENT FIELD NOTES

Wednesday, October 21, 2026
◆
First-hand AI deployment notes
◆
Issue 009

AI Adoption · Stalled Rollouts · Usage Rate

## Rolled Out AI and Nobody Uses It? The Problem Usually Isn't the AI. Work Backward From the One Task Employees Actually Do Every Day

Think BIG Content Team  |  October 21, 2026

When AI rollouts go unused, it's rarely because the model isn't smart enough. More often, nobody decided what it was for, nobody showed employees how to use it, and it never made it into the daily work. The fix: work backward from one task employees actually do every day.

## 1.  What's happening: bought, installed, activated, and then ignored

Plenty of companies have been through this. The boss sees how impressive AI is, buys a tool, sets up accounts, and holds a kickoff session. Two or three weeks later, employees are still doing things the old way, and hardly anyone clicks into the AI.

It isn't just a few companies. Surveys in Taiwan and abroad show the same pattern:

Taiwan: the biggest roadblock is "we don't know what to use it for."  As reported by Taiwanese media, the 2025 Survey on AI Use Among Small and Medium Enterprises , commissioned by Taiwan's Small and Medium Enterprise and Startup Administration (Ministry of Economic Affairs) and conducted by the Industrial Technology Research Institute, collected 1,207 valid responses from companies with 199 or fewer employees. The top challenge SMEs cited when considering AI was "no clear use case yet," followed by not understanding AI, high costs, talent shortages, and difficulty measuring results. The same survey found that only about 15% of SMEs have AI talent, and roughly 75% of that talent are entry-level users of off-the-shelf tools. (Source: [China Times Want Rich, 2025-12-26](https://wantrich.chinatimes.com/news/20251226900494-420501))

Globally: most companies haven't seen results yet.  An international management consulting firm surveyed 1,000 senior executives in 2024 and found that 74% of companies had yet to show tangible value from AI. Only 26% had built the capabilities to move beyond proofs of concept and generate real value. (Source: [BCG press release, 2024-10-24](https://www.bcg.com/press/24october2024-ai-adoption-in-2024-74-of-companies-struggle-to-achieve-and-scale-value))

People are using AI, just not the company's.  A large software company's 2024 survey of 31,000 knowledge workers in 31 markets found that 75% already use generative AI at work, but 78% of those users bring their own AI tools. Only 39% of people who use AI at work have received AI training from their company. (Source: [Microsoft Work Trend Index 2024](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/worklab/work-trend-index/ai-at-work-is-here-now-comes-the-hard-part))

Put the three together and the picture is clear: employees aren't refusing AI. The setup their company handed them just doesn't connect to the work they actually do every day.

## 2.  The debate: is the problem the AI, or the people and processes?

Those who say it's about processes and organization  have plenty of evidence. In the same report, the consulting firm describes a "10-20-70" principle: leading companies put 10% of their resources into algorithms, 20% into technology and data, and 70% into people and processes. (Source: [BCG press release](https://www.bcg.com/press/24october2024-ai-adoption-in-2024-74-of-companies-struggle-to-achieve-and-scale-value))

A 2025 preliminary report from a research initiative at MIT reached a similar conclusion. As reported by Fortune , it found that most companies' generative AI efforts were falling short, and that the key issue wasn't the quality of the AI models but a "learning gap" between tools and organizations, along with flawed enterprise integration. (Source: [Fortune, 2025-08-18](https://fortune.com/2025/08/18/mit-report-95-percent-generative-ai-pilots-at-companies-failing-cfo/))

Skeptics raise two cautions:  1. Read the numbers carefully.  The MIT report is preliminary research, and coverage describes its sample and methods inconsistently. It shouldn't be taken as proof that every AI project fails. 2. Tools still matter.  If an AI often gets answers wrong, gives no sources, or responds slowly, employees will try it once or twice and stop. No amount of training can save a tool that isn't good enough.

The two views don't conflict: a good-enough tool is the baseline. Once you clear that bar, what decides whether people use it is where it's used, who uses it, and how.

◆ First-hand notes

## 3. What we've learned doing this work

Think BIG deploys AI agents for businesses and keeps reviewing usage logs after handover. Here's what we've learned, with no client details:

1. Unused systems all show similar symptoms.  Employees stick with the old way. They ask once, get a wrong answer, and never ask again. The entry point is buried behind several logins. Nobody knows what to ask. Answers come without sources, so people don't dare rely on them. Permissions are misconfigured, so people can't see documents they should. Almost none of this has anything to do with how smart the model is.

2. Work backward from one task, not forward from a pile of features.  Before we start, we look for a task that meets three conditions: it happens every day, its rules can be written down, and the cost of a wrong answer is manageable. Think "sales looking up product specs" or "new hires checking internal policies." Get that one task used every day first, then move to the second.

3. Write acceptance questions the way employees actually ask.  We prepare a set of acceptance questions with known answers, phrased as closely as possible to how employees really talk, including abbreviations, casual wording, even typos. A system that aces neatly worded test questions but stumbles on real ones is a very common gap.

4. Put the AI where employees already are.  Every new website or account adds friction. When the AI lives inside a chat tool or system employees already use daily, usage tends to be much better. One caveat: when you connect an outside chat channel such as LINE, messages through that channel pass through that service, so make that clear before rollout.

5. Say "I don't know" when it doesn't know, and cite sources when it does.  Whether employees use it comes down to trust. When an answer shows which document it came from, employees can click through and check. Saying "I couldn't find that" builds more trust than making something up.

6. After handover, review the logs every week.  What employees asked, which questions got weak answers, which documents need to be added: it's all in the logs. Name one internal point person to spend a little time each week reviewing logs and adding material, and the system gets more accurate the more it's used. That's also the most practical way to close the "learning gap" mentioned above.

Our biggest takeaway: whether an AI rollout succeeds is often decided before the work begins.  Get clear on which one task the AI is for, and most of the later problems disappear.

## 4.  Our recommendations: answer these five questions before you roll out

1. What's the most time-consuming, most annoying task employees do every day?  Ask the front line directly, not just managers. 2. Does that task follow rules?  Work with documentation and standard answers is the best first job for an AI agent. 3. What happens if the answer is wrong?  Start with tasks where mistakes are manageable. For high-stakes work like external quotes or legal judgments, have the AI draft and a person confirm. 4. Where will employees use it?  Put it inside tools they already use, and open as few new entry points as possible. 5. Who reviews the logs and adds material?  Name one internal point person. They don't need to be technical, but they need to know the process and be able to make decisions.

Start with features Work backward from one task
Starting point What the tool can do What frustrates employees every day

First month Lots of features; nobody knows where to start One task used by someone every day

Acceptance Judged on the demo Tested with questions employees actually ask

After handover Nobody reviews logs; usage fades Weekly log reviews and new material; it gets more accurate over time

Bottom line: if nobody uses your AI, don't swap the AI first. Swap the question.

Further reading: if nobody inside your company can own the work of wiring AI into your processes, see [Think BIG NEWS Issue 007, "What Is a Forward Deployed Engineer?"](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/fde-outsourced-engineer-20261013/), on how small businesses can fill that gap with an embedded-style approach.

◆ Editor's Note · How Think BIG Approaches This

## Start with one task. Frozen scope. Delivery within 30 days.

(The following reflects Think BIG's own position and is separate from the neutral reporting above.)

We act as a company's remote FDE (embedded engineering) team, using TB FRAME, our four-stage method (assess, build, verify, maintain), to wire AI agents into your work: Start with one task:  during assessment, we identify the one rule-based task employees actually do every day, then decide what the AI agent will and won't do. Frozen scope, delivery within 30 days:  scope and acceptance questions are written down before work starts, and delivery happens within 30 days once scope is frozen and data is in place. Acceptance in your employees' words:  we test against known answers before handover; answers cite sources, and the agent says "I don't know" when it can't find something. First year of maintenance:  all three plans include first-year maintenance; after handover, we keep reviewing logs, adding material, and sending proactive alerts.

We don't promise sales results. We promise to wire AI into your actual work and let you see that it's running.

### FAQ

Q1: Why don't employees use AI after the company rolls it out?
The most common reason isn't that the AI isn't smart enough. It's that nobody decided which task the AI was for, nobody taught employees how to use it, and it never became part of the daily workflow. Answers without sources and hard-to-find entry points also make employees give up after a try or two.
Q2: What's the biggest barrier to AI adoption for small businesses in Taiwan?
According to media reports on the 2025 Survey on AI Use Among Small and Medium Enterprises, commissioned by Taiwan's Small and Medium Enterprise and Startup Administration and conducted by the Industrial Technology Research Institute, the top challenge SMEs cite when considering AI is "no clear use case yet," followed by not understanding AI, high costs, talent shortages, and difficulty measuring results.
Q3: Where should an AI rollout start?
With one task: find work employees repeat every day, whose rules can be written down, and where a wrong answer is manageable, such as looking up product specs or internal policies. Get that task used every day, then expand to a second.
Q4: How can you tell whether an AI rollout actually worked?
Don't judge by the demo. Build acceptance questions in the words employees really use, and confirm that answers are correct, cite sources, and say "I don't know" when nothing is found. After handover, keep reviewing usage logs to see whether people use it and which questions get weak answers.
Q5: Will employees avoid AI because they're worried about their jobs?
They might, which is why communication matters. Start with the repetitive, time-consuming work employees find most frustrating, so the AI saves them time, rather than starting with work that depends on their professional judgment. When employees see AI lightening their own load, they're usually much more willing to use it.

# AI Is Being Used to Automate Attacks — Could Your Tools Become Someone Else's Entry Point? | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Field Notes · Issue 010
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

AI DEPLOYMENT FIELD NOTES

Saturday, October 24, 2026
◆
First-hand AI deployment notes
◆
Issue 010

AI Security · Automated Attacks · Permissions

## AI Is Being Used to Automate Attacks — Could Your Tools Become Someone Else's Entry Point?

Think BIG Content Team  |  October 24, 2026

Microsoft's latest investigation documents attackers using AI to accelerate existing attack workflows. For organizations, the immediate questions are which tools can read data or take action, and who approves and owns that access.

## One. The Phenomenon: Some Attacks Reached Privileged Access in Less Than Three Hours

On October 21, 2026 , Microsoft reported that the threat actor it tracks as Storm-0940  had used the agentic AI penetration-testing framework ARTEX  to automate attacks as early as September that year. In multiple instances, the time from initial targeting to privileged access to an organization's cloud infrastructure was less than 3 hours .[1]

The report describes abuse of existing application access and credentials. It also cautions that an affected application's presence or successful attacker authentication does not itself establish data access or exfiltration .[1] Attack attempts, successful authentication, privileged access, and data exfiltration should therefore be distinguished.

A separate development provides context for the developer ecosystem. The Linux Foundation announced the formation of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)  on December 9, 2025 , with founding project contributions including Model Context Protocol (MCP), goose, and AGENTS.md.[2] This is background on open-source collaboration and governance, rather than an event coinciding with the attack disclosure.

Skills also need a concrete definition. The official anthropics/skills  repository on GitHub describes Skills in its README as folders containing instructions, scripts, and resources.[4] Our recommendation is to inventory skill contents, execution environments, and the accounts and permissions actually used as separate items.

## Two. Perspectives: What the Official Documents Emphasize

Microsoft: inspect application identities and subsequent activity.

Microsoft recommends reviewing service-principal sign-ins, unexpected credential or privilege changes, and applying least privilege.[1] We recommend including application permissions and activity records in deployment acceptance checks.

The Linux Foundation: support collaboration through open governance.

The AAIF announcement emphasizes a neutral, open environment and the development of tools, standards, and community collaboration.[2] Our interpretation is that foundation governance and deployment security reviews need separate treatment: project membership alone does not establish security certification for an individual package.

NIST: do not grant implicit trust based on network location.

In Zero Trust Architecture , the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) explains that assets and accounts should not receive implicit trust solely because of their physical or network location or ownership. Authentication and authorization precede establishment of a session to an enterprise resource.[3]

The documents have different purposes. We recommend turning their guidance into a deployment checklist: which identity executes, which resources it can access, who approves that access, and how activity is recorded.

## Three. Our First-Hand Lessons (Anonymized): Make Permissions Verifiable

When discussing an AI agent deployment, we start with two questions:

"What can it do to my data?"
"Who approves and maintains it, and who handles an incident?"

The following presents the team's practical views and recommendations without identifying clients. It is not evidence of customer outcomes or industry statistics.

### Lesson one: map permissions before choosing tools

We advocate starting with an inventory containing at least four fields: tool or skill name, data and operation scope, user or execution identity, and owner .

Break down the scope further: which files it may read, whether it may modify or delete them, whether it may call external services, and whether it may send data. Compare intended use with actual settings before deciding which capabilities to retain or change.

### Lesson two: document approval, maintenance, and response responsibilities

We recommend recording an approver, maintainer, and incident contact for each tool, together with a way to disable it or revoke access.

For operations that write, delete, or send important data externally, agree before deployment whether human review is required and who performs it. A named owner should have explicit duties and authority.

### Lesson three: define the period, calculation, and threshold for each metric

We recommend recording three metrics: usage count, the proportion of answers usable without editing, and the number of authorized tasks actually completed .

Agree on the measurement period, calculation method, and acceptance threshold before a trial. If results fall short, inspect data quality, permissions, workflow design, and usage records. Avoid judging success solely by a fixed number of days or whether a metric grows.

## Four. Our Recommendations: Three Things First

1. Start an inventory using existing documents

List the AI skills, tools, and extensions in use, including employee-installed items. Define the scope and identify the system administrators whose help is needed before scheduling the work and assigning staff.

Alongside names, record data and operation scope, execution identity, and ownership. Go beyond asking whether AI is in use.

2. Review data access, operation permissions, and provenance individually

- Unclear provenance or authorization:  pause new access grants and sensitive-data input while the owner investigates; restrict connections or disable the tool if necessary.

- Clear purpose but excessive permissions:  establish required functions in a test environment, then reduce permissions and verify the workflow.

- Clear purpose, permissions, and ownership:  retain records and agree on a review date and incident procedure.

If an incident is suspected, preserve records and carry out necessary containment in parallel. A routine inventory should not substitute for an incident investigation.

3. Document ownership and access revocation

Assign an owner to each retained tool. Record contact details, who can revoke access, and the order of response actions. If related tools share an owner, list exactly which tools that arrangement covers.

## Editor's Note · How Think BIG Approaches This: Make Deployment Verifiable

(The following presents Think BIG's practical position and recommendations.)

We advocate organizing AI agent deployment into assessment, building, verification, and operations:

- Assessment:  inventory tools, data, execution identities, and responsibilities before setting the deployment scope.

- Building:  configure permissions around actual needs; agree on human review and access revocation for important operations.

- Verification:  test known-answer questions and explicit tasks, checking sources, activity records, and permission boundaries.

- Operations:  specify service scope, duration, response arrangements, and fees in each proposal, together with log reviews and incident reporting.

Our position is to make permitted actions, approval, and stopping procedures verifiable deliverables, providing a basis for deployment and ongoing management.

### FAQ

Q1: What matters about AI automation in this report? Microsoft documents Storm-0940 using ARTEX to accelerate attacks, including multiple instances of less than 3 hours from initial targeting to privileged cloud access.[1] That finding has a defined scope; it does not establish that all attacks are now autonomously completed by AI. Q2: Should small and midsize businesses inventory their tools too? We recommend identifying tools, data, permissions, and owners, then prioritizing by data sensitivity and operational impact. Plan staffing, time, and technical assistance around the actual environment. Q3: How can we check whether an AI tool sends data externally? We recommend comparing product documentation, permission settings, external-service lists, and execution records. Where needed, ask technical staff to observe data flows in a test environment. After changing permissions, verify the functions that must remain available. Q4: How should employee-installed AI tools be managed? We recommend defining allowed installations, a declaration process, and sensitive-data rules. Restrict sensitive-data input to tools whose provenance or authorization remains unclear until an owner completes the review. Q5: Are all AI agents always on and able to send data proactively? This article does not treat every product as the same deployment type. Check individually whether execution is scheduled, which tools can be called, whether data can be written or sent externally, and which operations require human approval. Q6: What can we do when a related attack is suspected? Microsoft recommends preserving sign-in and audit records, inspecting service-principal activity and unexpected credential or privilege changes, and revoking unnecessary permissions and rotating credentials when suspicious activity is confirmed.[1] Authorized responders should act within the incident's scope, preserving evidence without delaying necessary containment.

# Give Your Local AI Too Much "Memory" and It Can Drag Down the Whole Machine — How to Size the Context Length | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Local AI Deployment Notes · Issue 011
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

LOCAL AI DEPLOYMENT NOTES

October 27, 2026   Tuesday
◆
Local AI Deployment Notes
◆
Issue 011

Local AI · Context Length · Memory Management

## Give Your Local AI Too Much “Memory” and It Can Drag Down the Whole Machine — How to Size the Context Length

Think BIG Content Team  |  October 27, 2026

If a local AI keeps getting slower and the rest of the computer bogs down with it, an unused GPU is one suspect. An oversized context length is another. Run ollama ps  and check two columns, PROCESSOR and CONTEXT, to see how much context is actually allocated and whether the model has spilled onto the CPU.

(We use the open-source tool Ollama as the example because its documentation spells out the defaults and the checks clearly. Other local runtimes work along similar lines under different setting names.)

This piece pairs with our Issue 2, “Running a Model Locally: Is Your GPU Actually Doing Anything?” Issue 2 covered models that never touch the GPU. This one covers the other case: the GPU is in use, but the context is set so large that memory runs out. Both start with the same command.

## One.  What’s Happening: Context Takes Memory Too

Context length is how much material the model can carry while it answers, measured in tokens. Ollama defines it as the maximum number of tokens the model has access to in memory.[2]

It isn’t free. Ollama’s documentation states that a larger context length increases the memory needed to run a model, and that you should make sure you have enough VRAM before raising it.[2] The FAQ adds that when a model serves several requests at once, required memory scales with parallel requests multiplied by context length; the default for parallel requests is 1.[1]

Watch the default.  Ollama’s FAQ says the default context window is 4,096 tokens.[1] The separate “Context length” page describes VRAM-based defaults instead: 4k below 24 GiB, 32k from 24 to 48 GiB, and 256k at 48 GiB or more.[2] Because the two pages differ, we don’t rely on either from memory. We read the CONTEXT column in ollama ps  and go by what the machine has actually allocated.[2]

Changing it is documented too. To change the server-wide default, set the OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH  environment variable. To change it for one model or one session, use /set parameter num_ctx  in the CLI, or pass num_ctx  in the API options.[1]

## Two.  Perspectives: Go Big, or Stay Stable?

The case for larger contexts:  Ollama’s “Context length” page recommends at least 64,000 tokens for context-heavy tasks such as web search, agents, and coding tools. The same page says that for best performance you can use a model’s maximum context length while avoiding offloading the model to the CPU.[2]

The case for counting the cost:  The FAQ explains that Flash Attention can significantly reduce memory use as context grows, and that the K/V cache (where context is held) can be quantized. q8_0  uses roughly half the memory of f16 , and q4_0  roughly a quarter, but precision loss may be more noticeable at larger context sizes, and the impact depends on the model and task.[1]

These views don’t really conflict. The documentation’s assumption throughout is that the model fits: open the context up, but check the memory budget first and confirm nothing has been pushed to the CPU.[2]

◆ First-Hand Notes

## Three. What We’ve Learned in Practice

These are observations from our own local AI agent deployments. They are not industry statistics and don’t describe any specific site.

1. “It’s getting slower — is the GPU too old?” is a common question. The common answer is configuration.  A pattern we see often: someone raises the context sharply so the AI “remembers more,” memory can’t hold it, part of the model ends up on the CPU, and response times stretch out.

2. Be extra careful on unified-memory machines.  When the graphics chip and the system share one pool of memory, context isn’t only eating “the GPU’s share.” The symptoms we commonly see: responses get progressively slower, the whole computer turns sluggish, and the disk starts writing heavily to swap. At that point it isn’t just the AI that’s slow; every other program is being held back too.

3. Measure the need before picking a number.  We don’t start with a fixed figure. The steadier sequence is to run a few real tasks, see how many tokens each actually sends, and then decide how much headroom to leave. Ollama’s API responses include prompt_eval_count , the number of input tokens in that request, which is a good enough basis.[3]

4. Check CONTEXT and PROCESSOR before handover.  In ollama ps , PROCESSOR shows 100% GPU, 100% CPU, or a split between them;[1] CONTEXT shows the allocated context length.[2] We screenshot both columns at handover.

## Four.  Our Recommendations: Three Steps

1. Measure, then set.  Take the three to five tasks you run most often (answering support emails, summarizing meeting notes, searching internal documents), run each a few times, and record prompt_eval_count .[3] Take the highest value, add room for the answer, and start there.

2. Run ollama ps  right after any change.  If PROCESSOR shows any CPU share, the model plus its context no longer fits in VRAM.[1] Bring the context back down, or look at Flash Attention or K/V cache quantization. If you quantize, re-check quality on your real tasks.[1]

3. Size parallelism and context together.  If several people will use it at once, memory needs multiply.[1] Decide how many concurrent requests you need first, then set the context.

In short: a big context is fine if the machine can hold it.  If it can’t, the whole computer slows down with it.

◆ Editor’s Note · How Think BIG Approaches This: Settings With a Reason Behind Them

## Measure first, then set. Every setting should answer “why this number?”

(The following is Think BIG’s own practice, kept separate from the reporting above.)

When we deploy local AI agents, context length isn’t a guess: set from real workloads  — we measure input size on the client’s own tasks before fixing context length and parallelism; leave evidence at handover  — screenshots of the PROCESSOR and CONTEXT columns from ollama ps , handed to the owner with the settings; re-verify after changes  — after adjusting context, quantization, or parallelism, we rerun the same tasks to confirm speed and answer quality are still acceptable.

Our position: every setting should come with an answer to “why this number?” Issue 13 extends this to model selection, using the same logic as a foundation.

### Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What is context length?
The amount of material the AI can carry while it answers, counted in tokens. Ollama defines it as the maximum number of tokens the model has access to in memory.[2]
Q2: What is Ollama’s default context length?
The FAQ says 4,096 tokens; the “Context length” page describes VRAM-based defaults of 4k, 32k, or 256k.[1][2] Because they differ, check the CONTEXT column in ollama ps  for what your machine actually uses.[2]
Q3: How do I change it?
Use the OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH  environment variable for the server-wide default, and num_ctx  for a single model or request (/set parameter num_ctx  in the CLI, or the API options).[1]
Q4: Is a bigger context always better?
Ollama recommends at least 64,000 tokens for agents and coding tools, and also notes that larger contexts need more memory, so confirm you have enough VRAM.[2] Our advice is to measure your actual need first.
Q5: What if memory is tight but I need a longer context?
Ollama’s documentation points to Flash Attention and K/V cache quantization (q8_0  at roughly half, q4_0  at roughly a quarter of f16  memory). How much quantization affects quality depends on the model and task, so test it yourself.[1]
Q6: Is this the same problem as “the GPU isn’t being used”?
Not quite, but you check it the same way. Our Issue 2 covered a model not using the GPU; this article covers a context too large for memory. In both cases, start with the PROCESSOR column in ollama ps .[1]

Sources

    [2] Ollama, “Context length” (definition, VRAM-based defaults, recommendation for agent tasks, the CONTEXT column in ollama ps ); accessed October 24, 2026: [docs.ollama.com/context-length](https://docs.ollama.com/context-length)  ·

# Confidently Wrong: What We Learned When an AI Said Our AI Company Had Nothing to Do with AI | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Field Notes · Issue 006
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

被　AI　看見

October 12, 2026 · Monday
◆
First-hand observations on AI deployment
◆
Issue 006

AI Hallucinations · Verification Habits & Business Workflow

## Confidently Wrong: What We Learned When an AI Said Our AI Company Had Nothing to Do with AI

Think BIG Content Team  |  October 12, 2026

Training rewards guessing, not admitting uncertainty. Legal RAG tools still hallucinate on 17–33% of queries. Being pushed back makes AI more likely to flip from right to wrong. Verify important facts at the source.

## 1.  What's happening: AI sounds just as sure when it's wrong

A “hallucination” is AI-generated content that sounds plausible but isn’t true. The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) calls it confabulation  in its July 2024 generative AI risk profile: the production of confidently stated but erroneous or false content. ([NIST AI 600-1](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf)) The real problem isn’t that AI makes mistakes. It’s that the tone doesn’t change when it does.

Why does this happen?  In a September 2025 paper, Why Language Models Hallucinate , OpenAI researchers argue that standard training and evaluation procedures reward guessing rather than acknowledging uncertainty. ([arXiv 2509.04664](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04664), [OpenAI explainer](https://openai.com/index/why-language-models-hallucinate/)) Their analogy is a multiple-choice exam: guessing might pay off; leaving it blank guarantees zero. When models are graded on accuracy alone, the one that guesses looks better. Their comparison of two OpenAI models on the SimpleQA evaluation:

Model that abstains when unsure Model that answers nearly everything
Abstention rate 52% 1%

Accuracy 22% 24%

Error rate 26% 75%

Accuracy differs by just two points. The error rate is nearly three times higher. The paper also explains which facts are most at risk : spelling and grammar follow patterns, so errors fade as models scale. But arbitrary, rarely seen facts — like a specific person’s birthday, or a small company’s registered activities — can’t be inferred from patterns, and that’s where hallucinations show up.

Even with the right document in hand, AI can still drift.  Vectara’s Hallucination Leaderboard gives each model an article, tells it to summarize using only information provided, and checks whether the summary adds anything not in the source. The version updated September 22, 2026, tested on more than 7,700 articles, showed hallucination rates from about 1.8% to 24.2% across models. ([vectara/hallucination-leaderboard](https://github.com/vectara/hallucination-leaderboard)) These measure a summarization task, not general Q&A, and rankings shift as versions update. The point: even when you hand AI the correct document, it may still add things the document never said.

## 2.  What the research says in high-stakes fields

Law.  Stanford RegLab and Stanford HAI researchers tested well-known AI legal research tools on a preregistered set of more than 200 legal questions. These tools use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). They made fewer errors than general-purpose chatbots, but each tool still hallucinated on roughly 17% to 33% of queries. Published in the Journal of Empirical Legal Studies , 2025. ([Magesh et al., JELS 2025](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jels.12413), [arXiv 2405.20362](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20362)) The same group’s earlier work found general-purpose chatbots hallucinated on 58% to 82% of legal queries. ([Stanford HAI](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-trial-legal-models-hallucinate-1-out-6-or-more-benchmarking-queries))

Medical literature.  A 2024 study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research  asked three then-popular chatbots to find references for systematic reviews on rotator cuff conditions. Across 471 references, the share that either didn’t exist or had key details wrong was 28.6%, 39.6%, and 91.4% for the three models. Conclusion: every AI-generated reference needs to be checked. ([Chelli et al., JMIR 2024](https://www.jmir.org/2024/1/e53164))

Changing the answer under pressure is its own problem.  Anthropic researchers at ICLR 2024 tested five AI assistants: answer a question, then hear the user say, “I don’t think that’s right. Are you sure?” The assistants changed their original answer in roughly 32% to 86% of cases, and switching from correct to incorrect was more common than the reverse. The researchers call this sycophancy . ([Sharma et al., arXiv 2310.13548](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548))

There is good news.  The OpenAI paper argues hallucinations aren’t inevitable, because models can abstain when uncertain. A 2024 study in Nature  proposed a detection method: ask the model the same question several times; if the meanings of the answers don’t agree, that’s a sign it may be making things up. ([Farquhar et al., Nature 2024](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07421-0)) The broad consensus: hallucinations can be reduced and detected, but no current method makes them disappear.

◆ First-hand notes

## 3. What happened to us

On October 4, 2026, we asked an AI chatbot: “Which companies in Taiwan are deploying AI agents?” It listed a few. We weren’t on the list.

Then we asked about our own company. It answered with complete confidence: Think BIG Make it Real Co., Ltd. was registered only for event planning, performing arts, arts and culture, and software publishing, and had nothing to do with AI.

In fact, our registration with Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs lists 20 business activities, including I301010 Information Software Services and I301020 Data Processing Services. The items the chatbot named are on our registration, but they’re only part of it. The words “only” and “nothing to do with AI” were wrong.

When we pushed back, it immediately reversed itself and said we were an AI company.

Four lessons:

1. A confident tone doesn’t mean it checked.  The first answer had no hedging at all. It read as if it had seen our registration. It was incomplete, and its conclusion was wrong.

2. Changing its answer doesn’t make the second one right.  This time the second answer happened to be correct. But as the sycophancy research shows, AI is more likely to flip from right to wrong under pressure. Neither answer should be taken at face value.

3. Obscure facts are the most fragile.  A small company’s registered business activities are exactly the kind of rarely seen, pattern-free fact the OpenAI paper describes.

4. The original record is what you can trust.  To confirm a Taiwanese company’s registered activities, check the Ministry of Economic Affairs’ public company registry — that’s the version published by the registering authority.

## 4.  Our recommendations

For individuals: five habits

1. Verify important facts at the source.  Company details from the official registry, laws from the legal database, health questions with a doctor. AI is great for organizing and pointing you in a direction; it isn’t your final evidence. 2. Ask for sources, then open them.  In the medical study, a large share of AI-provided references didn’t exist. Confirm the source is real and says what the AI claims. 3. Say it outright: “If you’re not sure, say you don’t know.”  OpenAI’s comparison shows a model willing to abstain makes far fewer errors. 4. Ask more than once, or ask a different AI.  If the answers don’t line up, go back and verify. 5. Don’t treat a reversal as “finally right.”  Check both answers against the original source.

For businesses: build verification into the workflow

1. Have AI answer from your own documents (RAG), but don’t assume that makes it error-free.  Both the legal tools study and the summarization leaderboard show errors drop with source documents in hand, but not to zero. 2. Require a citation with every answer, linked back to the original.  Then a quick check takes seconds instead of a full re-research. 3. Make “I don’t know” an official answer.  Better for the AI to say “That’s not in our knowledge base” than to fill the gap on its own. 4. Put a human review step on high-risk output.  Contracts, quotes, public announcements, and anything regulatory should have key figures and facts confirmed before they go out. 5. Spot-check regularly.  Re-ask a set of questions with known answers and track accuracy and the “I don’t know” rate, especially after a model or data update.

Bottom line: sounding confident isn’t the same as being right.  Make verification a habit, and AI becomes genuinely useful.

◆ Editor’s note · How Think BIG approaches this

## Help AI describe you accurately. Help AI agents know what they don’t know.

(The following reflects Think BIG’s own position and is separate from the neutral reporting above.)

Having an AI misdescribe our own company registration was a useful reminder: AI assembles answers from whatever information it can find. If the correct information isn’t somewhere it can reach, it may confidently fill the gaps with an incomplete picture.

GEO (helping AI describe you accurately):  We help businesses write clear, consistent company information, service descriptions, and FAQs, and publish them where AI systems can find them, to improve the chances that AI describes you correctly. We focus on being seen and described accurately; we don’t promise specific rankings or sales results.

AI agent deployment (knowledge base + verification):  When we set up AI agents for a business, we have them look up the company’s own documents before answering, cite their sources, and say “I don’t know” when the answer isn’t there. Before handover, we test with a set of questions that have known answers to confirm the agent both cites and declines when it should.

Hallucinations can’t be fully eliminated today. But you can design a process that makes them less frequent and easier to catch.

### FAQ

Q1: What is an AI hallucination?
An AI hallucination is content an AI generates that sounds plausible but is false or doesn’t exist, usually delivered in the same confident tone as a correct answer. NIST calls it confabulation: confidently stated but erroneous or false content.
Q2: Why does AI sound so sure when it’s wrong?
A 2025 OpenAI paper argues that training and evaluation work like a multiple-choice exam: guessing can earn points, while “I don’t know” earns zero, so models learn to guess. Rarely seen facts, like a small company’s registration details, are especially likely to come out wrong.
Q3: If an AI changes its answer after I push back, can I trust the new answer?
Not necessarily. Research at ICLR 2024 found that AI assistants often change their answers when asked “Are you sure?”, and switching from correct to incorrect is more common than the reverse. Check both answers against the original source.
Q4: If AI answers from our own documents using RAG, will it stop hallucinating?
It will hallucinate less, but not zero. The legal AI tools in the Stanford study all used this kind of approach and still hallucinated on roughly 17% to 33% of queries. Pair it with citations, an explicit “I don’t know” rule, and human review.
Q5: How can I check what a Taiwanese company is actually registered to do?
Search the company name or tax ID on the Ministry of Economic Affairs’ public company registration lookup at [findbiz.nat.gov.tw](https://findbiz.nat.gov.tw/). It shows the business activities as published by the registering authority, which is more reliable than any AI or third-party summary.

# Who Does ChatGPT Cite When It Answers Questions About Taiwan? Where Local Brands Should Put Their Information | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Field Notes · Issue 005
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

被　AI　看見

October 11, 2026 · Sunday
◆
First-hand observations on AI deployment
◆
Issue 005

GEO Source Analysis · Local Brand Placement

## Who Does ChatGPT Cite When It Answers Questions About Taiwan? — Where Local Brands Should Put Their Information

Think BIG Content Team  |  October 11, 2026

15,729 citations reveal: ChatGPT leans on brand sites and government bodies, roughly 70% not in Chinese. Perplexity leans toward social and video. Three AIs, three separate playing fields — local brands need a separate plan for each.

## 1.  What's happening: same question in Chinese, three completely different source lists

In July 2026, an independent study in Taiwan published a rare dataset. The researcher wrote 60 consumer-decision questions in Traditional Chinese, sent them through the APIs of three AI services (ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity), repeated each question multiple times, and collected 15,729 citations, each tagged by source type and language. (Source: [Taiwan Traditional Chinese AI citation study, July 2026](https://geoiscool.com/ai-citation-taiwan/))

Source types cited by each AI (selected)

Source type ChatGPT Gemini Perplexity
Brand websites 55.8% 35.5% 18.6%

Government / research institutions 21.2% 1.3% 0.7%

Review and comparison sites 6.1% 20.5% 21.4%

News media 1.4% 12.0% 8.8%

Forums 7.4% 3.2% 10.8%

Social media 0.1% 0.1% 7.9%

Video 0.0% 1.4% 6.7%

Language of cited content

Language ChatGPT Gemini Perplexity
Traditional Chinese (Taiwan) 30.1% 71.4% 87.8%

English 44.4% 18.1% 5.5%

Japanese 23.1% 4.3% 1.5%

Two more findings stand out: ChatGPT doesn’t always search.  It triggered a web search on only 46% of questions and answered the rest from model memory with no sources. For brand-comparison questions, though, the trigger rate rose to 70%. Three AIs, three separate playing fields.  ChatGPT’s cited domains overlapped only 5.4% with Perplexity’s and 6.3% with Gemini’s. Perplexity and Gemini overlapped just 20.1%.

Read these numbers with their limits in mind.  This is independent, non-peer-reviewed research. It used APIs, not the consumer interface. It ran in a single time window in July 2026. Questions were consumer decisions; the researcher notes ChatGPT frequently cited official U.S. and Japanese government sites, so results for business-services questions may differ. Use it for direction, not as a law for every industry.

## 2.  What the sources say: why does ChatGPT lean so hard on official sources?

Other research points the same way.  An April 2026 study across ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews/Gemini, and Perplexity analyzed 602 prompts and more than 21,000 citations. It found that Perplexity and Google cite more sources, more broadly, while ChatGPT cites fewer but each page it reads carries more influence on the answer. High-impact sources tended to be longer, well structured, and closely relevant to the question. ([arXiv 2604.25707](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25707))

Whether ChatGPT searches determines whether you can influence it.  A 2026 University of St. Gallen study found that 57.8% of ChatGPT’s runs had no citations at all, because it triggers web search only for certain queries. ([arXiv 2604.07585](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07585)) When it doesn’t search, it relies on what it learned in training — and what shapes those answers is consistent public information across many sites over time, not the web page you updated yesterday.

What the platforms say.  OpenAI: ChatGPT search builds its index with OAI-SearchBot, and sites that block it won’t appear in ChatGPT search answers. ([OpenAI crawler overview](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots), [Help Center](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9237897-chatgpt-search)) Google: AI Overviews and AI Mode draw on Google’s own index; one of Google’s recommended practices is keeping Merchant Center and Google Business Profile information up to date. ([Google Search Central](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)) Perplexity: its index is built by PerplexityBot, which Perplexity says is not used to crawl content for training AI models. ([Perplexity crawler docs](https://docs.perplexity.ai/guides/bots))

Forum buzz can’t be manufactured.  Perplexity does cite forums and social media, but paying for forum recommendations is a dead end. Dcard permanently bans accounts used for word-of-mouth marketing or brand promotion, and an undisclosed paid endorsement in a consumer’s voice may violate Taiwan Fair Trade Commission rules on endorsement advertising. ([Dcard rules](https://www.dcard.tw/f/announcement/p/234243656), [Taiwan FTC guidelines](https://www.ftc.gov.tw/internet/main/doc/docDetail.aspx?uid=165&docid=13021)) What does work: posting genuinely useful content from your own named accounts.

◆ First-hand notes

## 3. What we changed after reading the study

Our business is in Taiwan, and we’ve always published primarily in Chinese. The biggest takeaway for us: if most of what ChatGPT cites for Taiwan questions isn’t in Chinese, a Chinese-only website starts at a disadvantage there.

Here’s what we did:

1. An English edition of every NEWS article.  Starting this week, every article ships with an English version, and the two pages are linked with hreflang so AI systems know they cover the same topic. The English version isn’t a word-for-word translation; it’s rewritten for English-speaking readers.

2. One consistent official identity.  Our legal name, English name, business registration number, location, and service description now read the same across our website, social bios, and listings. Our company registration with Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs is already public government data, and the description on our website matches it.

3. A separate plan per AI, not one-size-fits-all.  Our website and English pages for ChatGPT; site structure and Google Business Profile for Gemini and Google AI Mode; long-form posts on our own named social accounts for Perplexity.

4. Still in progress:  listings in industry association and public directories, and bylined media coverage. We’re building these from a low starting point, and we won’t use fake accounts or paid posts to fill the gap faster.

An AI once told us, with total confidence, that our company had nothing to do with AI. Looking back, it most likely couldn’t find enough consistent information about us and pieced together fragments. Making our identity consistent across multiple trustworthy places is, in our view, the first thing worth doing.

## 4.  Our recommendations: a per-AI placement plan for local brands

Start with which AI your customers use, then decide where to put your information.  The table below reflects the study’s observations; treat it as direction, and measure your own industry.

To get mentioned by It tends to cite Where to put your information
ChatGPT Brand websites, government and research institutions; high share of English A bilingual website with Chinese and English pages linked to each other; government and industry association directories; institutional-style content such as method write-ups and white papers

Gemini / Google AI Mode Brand websites, review sites, news media A website Google can index and show snippets for; Google Business Profile; bylined media coverage and review-site listings

Perplexity Review sites, brand websites, forums and social, video Long-form posts from your own named social accounts (e.g., Threads); YouTube videos with transcripts; third-party comparison lists

Four things that help with every AI:

1. Keep your name, address, phone number, and registration number consistent.  Decide how your Chinese name, English name, and short name are written, and use them everywhere. 2. Use Taiwanese terminology and Taiwan-specific details.  Traditional Chinese, local wording, a full address, a +886 phone number, and your registration number all tell AI you’re a Taiwanese business. 3. Publish brand-comparison content.  ChatGPT searches most often on brand-comparison questions, so neutral “A vs. B” pages have the best chance of being read. Stick to facts. 4. Put important information in text on the page.  Not only in images, PDFs, or collapsed tabs.

Bottom line: not every AI reads the same sources.  Find out which AI your customers ask, then put accurate information where that AI looks.

◆ Editor’s note · How Think BIG approaches this

## Measure first. Three AIs, three plans. Compliant channels only.

(The following reflects Think BIG’s own position and is separate from the neutral reporting above.)

In our search visibility service (SEO + GEO), recommendations are always written separately for each AI: Measure first, then place  — we use repeated sampling to see where you stand on each AI and which sources each one cites, then decide where to invest first. Three AIs, three plans  — ChatGPT: your website (including English pages) and institutional directories. Gemini and Google AI Mode: site structure, Google Business Profile, and bylined coverage. Perplexity: named social accounts and video.

Consistent identity is the foundation.  We align your company name, description, and contact details everywhere, so AI can recognize you and describe you correctly. Compliant channels only  — no paid forum posts, no fake accounts, no fake reviews; paid partnerships are always disclosed.

We don’t promise rankings or sales results. We promise to put the right information in the right places and show you the numbers every month.

### FAQ

Q1: What sources does ChatGPT cite most when answering questions about Taiwan?
According to a July 2026 Taiwan study (60 consumer-decision questions, 15,729 citations), 55.8% of ChatGPT’s citations were brand websites and 21.2% were government or research institutions, about 77% combined. Blogs and news media made up very small shares. It’s an independent, single-window, API-based study, and results may vary by industry.
Q2: Why does ChatGPT cite English sources when the question is in Traditional Chinese?
In the same study, 44.4% of ChatGPT’s cited content was in English and 23.1% in Japanese, with only 30.1% in Traditional Chinese. The researcher observed frequent citations of official U.S. and Japanese government sites. For Taiwanese brands, a consistent English version of your website is an additional way to be read by ChatGPT.
Q3: Will posting recommendations about myself on Dcard or PTT improve AI visibility?
We don’t recommend it. Dcard permanently bans accounts used for word-of-mouth marketing or brand promotion, and an undisclosed paid endorsement in a consumer’s voice may violate Taiwan Fair Trade Commission rules. A better approach is sharing genuine, useful content from your own named accounts.
Q4: Do different AI services really cite different sources?
Yes, very different ones. The same study found ChatGPT’s cited domains overlapped only 5.4% with Perplexity’s and 6.3% with Gemini’s, and Perplexity and Gemini overlapped just 20.1%. Being visible on one AI doesn’t mean you’re visible on another, so placement and measurement both need to be done separately.
Q5: What should a local small business do first?
Make your company identity consistent online: Chinese and English names, address, phone number, registration number, and service description should read the same on your website, Google Business Profile, social bios, and public directories. It’s low-cost and helps both Google Search and every AI recognize you.

# What Is a Forward Deployed Engineer, and Why Is It AI's Most Wanted Role? What Small Businesses Can Do Without an FDE Budget | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Field Notes · Issue 007
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

被　AI　看見

October 13, 2026 · Tuesday
◆
First-hand observations on AI deployment
◆
Issue 007

AI Deployment · Embedded Engineering · Small Business

## What Is a Forward Deployed Engineer, and Why Is It AI’s Most Wanted Role? — What Small Businesses Can Do Without an FDE Budget

Think BIG Content Team  |  October 13, 2026

An FDE works inside your systems and data to wire AI into your actual workflows. Job postings surged more than 800% in 2025, and in 2026 major companies invested billions. AI’s bottleneck has moved from building models to putting them to work.

## 1.  What's happening: AI's hottest job title is an engineer who gets sent out

FDE stands for forward deployed engineer. “Forward-deployed” comes from U.S. military jargon. ([Wikipedia, “Forward deployed engineer”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward_Deployed_Engineer)) The role was developed by a U.S. data analytics software company. In a 2019 blog post, the company explained the difference: software engineers build the core platform, one capability serving many customers; FDEs deploy the platform to customers, bringing many capabilities to bear on one customer’s critical problems, measuring success by impact on that customer’s goals. The post also addressed a common question: an FDE isn’t a consultant. Consultants typically deliver a one-time analysis or recommendation; FDEs deploy actual software and build long-term solutions together with the customer, doing significantly more engineering. ([“Dev versus Delta,” 2019](https://blog.palantir.com/dev-versus-delta-demystifying-engineering-roles-at-palantir-ad44c2a6e87))

Generative AI turned the title into a phenomenon. June 2025:  A U.S. venture capital firm called the FDE the hottest job in startups, reasoning that enterprises want AI but need someone to set it up; onboarding an AI agent is no different from onboarding a new employee. ([Andreessen Horowitz, 2025-06-04](https://a16z.com/services-led-growth/)) January–September 2025:  According to an analysis by Indeed and the Financial Times , FDE job postings grew more than 800%. (As reported by: [Salesforce blog, 2025-11-19](https://www.salesforce.com/blog/forward-deployed-engineer/)) 2026:  CNBC reported a major cloud provider investing $1 billion in a new forward deployed engineering unit ([CNBC, 2026-06-30](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/30/aws-amazon-ai-forward-deployed-engineers.html)), and a major software company committing $2.5 billion and 6,000 employees to a new AI implementation unit ([CNBC, 2026-07-02](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/02/microsoft-commits-2point5-billion-6000-employees-ai-implementation-unit.html)).

In short: AI’s bottleneck has moved from building models to putting them to work.  The FDE is the role that grew up in that gap.

## 2.  The debate: real need, or consulting with a new title?

Supporters  say FDEs solve the hardest part of AI. Models can be bought and swapped, but every company’s data, workflows, and no-fail rules are different. The same a16z piece points out that even model providers are hiring FDEs: as foundation models become more interchangeable, owning the application layer inside the customer’s workflow matters more. ([Andreessen Horowitz](https://a16z.com/services-led-growth/))

Skeptics  raise three points: “Isn’t this just consulting?”  KDnuggets used that as a headline; its answer lands in between: the title may splinter or fade, but the skill of deploying AI into real environments is here to stay. ([KDnuggets](https://www.kdnuggets.com/forward-deployed-engineer-ais-hottest-new-career-or-consulting-with-a-better-title)) It isn’t glamorous.  The Wall Street Journal  reported in March 2026 that some engineers see it as undesirable because of travel pressure and tight timelines. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward_Deployed_Engineer)) It’s expensive.  The a16z piece is literally titled “Trading Margin for Moat.” For large enterprises it’s an investment; for small businesses it’s often out of reach.

Both sides are really describing the same thing: deploying AI takes someone working inside your processes to get the job done.  In Taiwan, that’s especially pressing: the country has more than 1.715 million SMEs, over 98% of all businesses, providing nearly 80% of jobs. ([Taiwan MoEA, 2025 SME White Paper](https://www.moea.gov.tw/MNS/populace/news/News.aspx?kind=1&menu_id=40&news_id=121491)) Most of them can’t afford a full-time FDE, but they need AI wired into their daily work all the same.

◆ First-hand notes

## 3. What we've learned doing this work: the remote FDE

When Think BIG deploys AI agents for businesses, we do the FDE part: work inside your systems and data to connect AI to your workflows, then test, hand over, and maintain it. The difference is we work as remote FDEs : operating on your machines or cloud environment through secure remote access instead of stationing someone on site. Here’s what we’ve learned, with no client details:

1. Take inventory before building anything.  Many companies already have computers, cloud accounts, and some AI subscriptions. We always inventory existing equipment and accounts first, and reuse what works instead of buying twice.

2. Keep assets in your name.  Cloud resources, accounts, and data are always set up under the business’s own accounts. After we step back, the system is still yours, and nobody has you locked in.

3. Freeze the scope before work starts.  Before we begin, we write down which questions the AI must answer, which data it reads, and what it must never do, and we prepare a set of acceptance questions with known answers. For enterprise projects, delivery happens within 30 days once scope is frozen and data is in place. In our experience, an unclear scope is the most common reason projects drag on.

4. Disable outbound actions during testing.  While testing an AI agent, we block its ability to send email, publish posts, or write to external systems, and only turn those back on after its behavior checks out. No “oops, it actually sent that.”

5. Accept on evidence, not on “it’s done.”  For example: a local model confirmed to be running on the GPU, answers include citations, and the agent says “I don’t know” when it can’t find something. Each backed by test results, not a demo.

6. Make it visible after handover.  Once live, the system is monitored continuously and problems trigger alerts rather than failing silently. The worst failure mode for an AI agent is looking like it’s running when it stopped days ago.

Our biggest takeaway: an FDE’s value isn’t about being physically on site. It’s about someone owning the outcome.

## 4.  Our recommendations: how a small business without an FDE budget can close the gap

1. Pick one workflow before you pick a tool.  For example, auto-replies to common customer questions, or search across internal documents. The more specific the goal, the easier it is to verify. 2. Name one internal point person.  They don’t need to be technical, but they need to know the process, make decisions, and supply data. 3. Get the scope and acceptance questions in writing.  Agree up front on what’s in, what’s out, and which questions will be used to sign off. 4. Keep accounts, data, and systems in your own name.  Whoever you hire, make sure what’s delivered belongs to you. 5. Ask how it will be maintained after handover.  Who monitors it, how you’ll be notified, and how fast they respond. An AI agent isn’t install-and-forget software.

Hire a full-time FDE Remote, embedded-style deployment
Best for Companies running several AI workflows needing long-term in-house development Small and mid-sized businesses starting with one or a few workflows

On site Yes No; work happens over secure remote access

Scope Grows with the company’s needs Frozen up front; next steps evaluated after delivery

Watch out for Hard to recruit; needs someone to manage them Your point person must supply data and make decisions

Bottom line: AI deployment isn’t short on models. It’s short on people who wire them into the work.  If a full-time FDE isn’t in the budget, find an embedded-style team that owns the outcome.

◆ Editor’s note · How Think BIG approaches this

## Remote FDE: inside the workflow, frozen scope, delivered in 30 days, your assets.

(The following reflects Think BIG’s own position and is separate from the neutral reporting above.)

We position ourselves as a remote FDE (embedded engineering) team : delivering the work large companies use FDEs for, in a form small and mid-sized businesses can afford.

Inside the workflow:  We don’t hand over a recommendations deck and leave. We connect AI agents to your data and processes until they actually work. Frozen scope, delivery within 30 days:  Scope and acceptance questions are written down before work starts, and delivery happens within 30 days once scope is frozen and data is in place. Your assets:  Accounts, cloud resources, and data stay in your name, and the model can be chosen to fit your needs and changed later.

Evidence-based acceptance, monitored operation:  We test against known answers before handover, then monitor continuously with proactive alerts.

We don’t promise sales results. We promise to wire AI into your actual work and let you see that it’s running.

### FAQ

Q1: What is a forward deployed engineer (FDE)?
An FDE works on behalf of a software or AI company inside a customer’s systems and data, deploying, customizing, and connecting the product to real business processes. Success is measured by whether the customer’s goal is met, not by delivering a report.
Q2: How is an FDE different from a consultant?
According to the company that developed the title, consultants typically provide a one-time analysis or recommendation, while FDEs deploy actual software and build long-term solutions with the customer, doing far more engineering. Some commentators say the line is blurring, but building a working system is the core of the FDE role.
Q3: Why have FDE job postings surged recently?
Companies want to use AI but lack people who can connect it to their own data and workflows. According to an analysis by Indeed and the Financial Times , FDE job postings grew more than 800% from January to September 2025, and in 2026 several large cloud and software companies launched dedicated deployment units.
Q4: How can a small business deploy AI without budget for an FDE?
Start with one specific workflow, name an internal point person, and work with an embedded-style team that can operate remotely. Get the scope and acceptance questions in writing before work begins, keep accounts and data in your own name, and clarify how monitoring and maintenance will work after handover.
Q5: Is remote AI agent deployment safe?
It depends on how it’s done. Confirm that remote access is secure, that accounts and data are in your company’s name, that the AI’s ability to send email or publish is blocked during testing, and that monitoring and alerts are in place after handover. All of this should be agreed before work starts.
