# Asked AI Once and Called It? AI Answers Are Probabilities, Not Rankings: How to Measure GEO Properly | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Field Notes · Issue 004
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

被　AI　看見

October 9, 2026 · Friday
◆
First-hand observations on AI deployment
◆
Issue 004

GEO Measurement · AI Visibility

## Asked AI Once and Called It? — AI Answers Are Probabilities, Not Rankings: How to Measure GEO Properly

Think BIG Editorial  |  October 9, 2026

AI answers change every time. Re-ask the same question minutes apart and roughly two-thirds of the cited sources will be different. To know whether AI mentions you, ask repeatedly, track for weeks, and look at ranges — not single results.

## 1.  The problem: one screenshot proves nothing

“ChatGPT just recommended us!” “I asked three AIs and none of them mentioned us.” We hear both versions constantly. Behind each one is the same habit: ask once, treat it as the answer.  That works for traditional search, where the same keyword returns the same rankings minutes apart. AI doesn’t work that way.

A team at the University of St. Gallen published a paper in April 2026 titled “Don’t Measure Once,” studying this problem directly. From January to March 2026, they asked the same sets of questions to four AI search services (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Mode, Gemini) every day across four industries — 8 questions per industry — tracking continuously for 45–46 days and re-asking the same question up to 10 times within the same day. ([arXiv 2604.07585](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07585))

Key findings: day-to-day turnover is high.  Cited sources on consecutive days overlap only 34–42% on average. Same-day re-asks show the same instability:  re-asking minutes apart overlaps only 32–43% of cited sources — nearly the same as asking on different days. The researchers concluded the instability comes from how models generate text, not from external algorithm updates.

Brands are more stable than sources.  Brand mentions overlap 45–59% day-over-day, more than citation sources. Some questions are very stable, some aren’t at all.  Seeing just one or two questions reveals the personality of those questions, not your overall visibility.

AI doesn’t always search the web.  ChatGPT answered 57.8% of questions without any citations — because it only triggers web search for certain queries, and relies on model memory for the rest.

One line from the paper’s abstract fits as this article’s headline: AI search visibility should be described as a distribution , not a single data point .

## 2.  What the research says: how many times is enough?

The paper gives concrete thresholds.  To estimate “the rate at which a brand is mentioned” with enough stability (standard error below 0.10), you need at least 7 repetitions per question per day ; for citation sources, at least 8. For time, a single brand requires at least 10 consecutive days  to bring the standard error below 0.10, and 24 days to drop below 0.05. The authors recommend using a 2–4 week rolling window . They also advise: set a separate baseline for each AI, don’t average across AI tools; use brand mention rate as the primary signal and citation URL tracking as a diagnostic.

Repeated questioning also detects AI fabrications.  A 2024 Nature paper proposed: ask a model the same question multiple times; if the answers contradict each other, that’s a signal the model may be hallucinating. ([Farquhar et al., Nature 2024](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07421-0)) One answer is a sample; repetition reveals the real picture.

Technique effectiveness can only be demonstrated with rigorous measurement.  A 2026 review of 45 GEO studies found that low source overlap and high run-to-run variability are pervasive in commercial audits; and no technique has been shown to improve discoverability stably, long-term, or across platforms. ([arXiv 2607.14035](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14035)) If your measurement is noisy, you can’t tell whether a technique worked or you got a lucky sample.

But don’t break the rules to measure.  Google’s spam policies prohibit unauthorized automated queries to Google Search, including scraping for ranking data. The compliant path: use each AI’s official API, supplement with manual UI checks, and state which channel you used in every report.

Official data is now available.  Bing Webmaster Tools launched an AI Performance report in public preview in February 2026, showing how often your pages are cited in Copilot and Bing AI summaries, which pages are cited, and how that changes over time. ([Bing Webmaster Blog](https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/February-2026/Introducing-AI-Performance-in-Bing-Webmaster-Tools-Public-Preview))

◆ First-hand notes

## 3. Three mistakes we made measuring our own AI visibility

Before launching our AI visibility service, we measured our own website first. We made three mistakes. All three are now written into our methodology.

Mistake 1: running one round and thinking we saw the truth.  Our first baseline was one question, one ask, one round. We barely showed up anywhere and felt discouraged. Then we checked Google Search Console and saw several of our guide pages ranked on the first page for their target queries. After reading the St. Gallen study, we confirmed: one round is statistically insufficient for any conclusion, positive or negative.

Mistake 2: a dirty test environment pollutes results.  On October 4, 2026, we ran a proxy test using an internal AI tool and found it had read notes stored on the test computer and incorporated them into answers. The results looked uncannily accurate — but that’s not what regular users see. OpenAI’s documentation notes that when memory is enabled, ChatGPT may use stored memories to rewrite search queries. Rule established: all measurements run in a clean environment — logged out, no conversation history, no memory, fresh session.

Mistake 3: treating “mentioned,” “cited,” and “described correctly” as the same thing.  AI can mention your name without linking to your page. It can link to your page while describing you incorrectly. We experienced this firsthand — an AI stated with complete confidence that our company had nothing to do with AI. Now every run records four things separately: did AI search the web, did it mention us, did it cite our URL, did it describe us accurately.

Our revised methodology in brief:

Item Our current practice
Questions Layered by intent: broad, contextual, conditional, brand comparison, factual; 3–5 phrasings per intent, including English versions

Lock questions Freeze the question set once built; add but never edit, so comparisons are valid over time

Repetitions Each question, each AI, multiple times per day with at least 10 minutes between runs

Duration Consecutive days; report on a 2–4 week rolling window

Separation Separate baseline for each AI; no cross-AI averages

Recording Did it search; was brand mentioned; position in answer; was URL cited; was description accurate

Reporting Every figure includes a 95% confidence interval; overlapping intervals between periods = “stable,” not “growth”

Channel State API vs. UI for each measurement; no automated scraping of Google pages

## 4.  Six principles for checking AI visibility yourself

1. Ask the same question several different ways.  Think like a customer: “Which [service] companies do you recommend in [city]?” “What’s good for a five-person company?” “How does A compare to B?”

2. Ask each question at least 5–7 times.  Record how many of those times you were mentioned. Look at the rate, not just “yes or no.”

3. Use a clean environment.  Log out or use a private window, disable memory, start a fresh session. Otherwise you’re seeing a personalized answer, not a representative one.

4. Track four things separately.  Did it search the web; did it mention you; did it cite your URL; did it describe you accurately.

5. Track for at least two weeks before talking about trends.  One-day fluctuations are mostly noise. Look at each AI separately — don’t average across platforms.

6. Don’t scrape Google.  It violates Google’s policies. For large-scale measurement, use official APIs or work with a team that does it compliantly.

If you’re evaluating a GEO vendor, ask five questions: How many questions, how many phrasings? How many repetitions per question? How many consecutive days? API or UI? Do the numbers include confidence intervals?  If they can’t answer, discount the report.

Bottom line: AI answers are probabilities, not rankings.  One ask is luck. Doing it properly gives you data.

◆ Editor’s note · How Think BIG approaches this

## Honest numbers. Readable reports. Verifiable methods.

(The following reflects Think BIG’s own position and is separate from the neutral reporting above.)

Our AI visibility reports follow this methodology and lay the method open in every report:

One “denominator and method” page:  how many questions, how many phrasings, how many repetitions per day, how many days, which AIs, which channel — all stated. You can re-run any query and verify.

Trigger rate listed separately:  did AI search the web for this question? Questions AI doesn’t search require different interventions than ones it does search.

Description accuracy listed separately:  not just whether AI mentioned you, but whether what it said was true. Inaccuracies are logged and tracked for correction.

Separate recommendations per AI:  different AIs favor different sources, so recommendations are split by platform.

Tiered conclusions:  each finding is labeled [count], [comparison], or [inference]; overlapping confidence intervals between periods = “stable,” not “growth.”

We don’t promise rankings or sales. We promise honest numbers, readable reports, and methods you can verify.

### FAQ

Q1: Why does the same AI question get different answers each time?
AI models introduce randomness when generating answers, and the sources they cite change along with the answer. A 2026 University of St. Gallen study found that re-asking the same question minutes apart overlaps only about 32–43% of cited sources on average — roughly the same as asking on consecutive days. The instability comes from how models generate text, not from external algorithm changes.
Q2: How many times do I need to ask AI the same question to get a reliable result?
The same study estimates you need at least 7 repetitions per question per day for brand mention rates, or 8 for citation rates, to bring the standard error below 0.10. For tracking trends, you need at least 10 consecutive days. The authors recommend using a 2–4 week rolling window.
Q3: Can I write a script to automatically query Google AI Mode for measurement?
No. Google’s spam policies prohibit automated queries to Google Search without permission, including scraping for ranking data. The compliant approach is to use each AI’s official API alongside manual spot-checks, and to document which channel you used in your report.
Q4: What’s the difference between AI “mentioning” me and “citing” me?
A mention means your name appears in the answer. A citation means the answer links to your page as a source. They don’t always happen together — and even when both occur, the description of your company may still be inaccurate. Track them separately.
Q5: Is there an official tool to see how often AI cites my website?
Bing Webmaster Tools launched an AI Performance report in public preview in February 2026, showing how often your pages are cited in Copilot and Bing AI summaries. On the Google side, AI-driven traffic is rolled into the “Web” search type in Search Console and can’t be broken out separately.

Sources
    Schulte, Bleeker, Kaufmann, “Don’t Measure Once: Measuring Visibility in AI Search (GEO),” University of St. Gallen (April 2026): [arXiv 2604.07585](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07585)  ·
    Farquhar et al., “Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy,” Nature (2024): [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07421-0)  ·
    “Optimizing Visibility in Generative Engines: A Critical Survey of GEO (2023–2026)”: [arXiv 2607.14035](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14035)  ·
    Google Search spam policies (automated traffic; 2026-08-28): [developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)  ·
    Bing Webmaster Blog, “AI Performance” (2026-02-10): [blogs.bing.com](https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/February-2026/Introducing-AI-Performance-in-Bing-Webmaster-Tools-Public-Preview)  ·
    OpenAI Help Center, “Searching the web with ChatGPT”: [help.openai.com](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9237897-chatgpt-search)

This article combines industry reporting with Think BIG’s first-hand measurement experience. Data about our own site is shown only as relative observations. AI tools are not named, and nothing here is directed at any company or product.

# What Is ISO/IEC 42001? Documenting How a Business Governs AI | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

AI Deployment Field Notes · Issue 016
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

AI DEPLOYMENT FIELD NOTES

November 6, 2026  ·  Friday
◆
AI Deployment Field Notes
◆
Issue 016

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 · AI Governance · Management Systems

## What Is ISO/IEC 42001? Documenting How a Business Governs AI

Think BIG Media  |  November 6, 2026

Inventory AI uses, owners, and checks before discussing certification. A management system needs evidence from everyday work.

## One.  What’s Happening: AI Governance Is Becoming Subject to Independent Assessment

On September 5, 2025, the UK accreditation body UKAS said it was advancing accreditation work for ISO/IEC 42001 AI management system certification.[1] We use that institutional development to introduce business preparation. We do not present its historical progress as today’s status or rank certification bodies.

ISO describes ISO/IEC 42001:2023 as requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving an AI management system. It applies to organizations providing or using AI products and services.[2] A business does not need to train its own model to have AI uses worth inventorying.

ISO’s public explainer covers responsibility, risk, data and system management, oversight, and improvement.[3] Our reading is that an organization should be able to explain why a use is allowed and what happens when it goes wrong. This article introduces public guidance; it is not a clause-by-clause treatment of the full standard or a certification checklist.

## Two.  Perspectives: A Common Framework Helps; Certificates Need Context

The case for structure:  UKAS describes accreditation work as supporting consistency and credibility in AI certification.[1] ISO describes a management system in terms of policies, objectives, and processes.[2] In our view, this makes governance accountable rather than leaving each department to interpret it independently.

The limitation:  ISO explains that its framework supports compliance obligations while laws and regulations still apply.[3] A certificate therefore should not be read as evidence that every answer is accurate or every use has received legal review. Management processes and task-specific checks address different questions.

ISO develops standards; external certification bodies conduct certification. Accreditation formally recognizes a certification body’s competence.[4] Keep those roles distinct. Ask about the standard edition, certified organization, covered activities, and verification contact rather than simply asking whether a supplier “has ISO.”

Begin with a bounded use, such as internal document Q&A. Ask which documents are allowed, who maintains versions, what happens without evidence, and who can suspend use. This starts the governance discussion; it does not establish conformity with the whole standard.

For external descriptions, distinguish completed work from plans. Completed checks need records; open items need owners and actions. Planning around a standard should not be worded as completed independent certification. Keep the wording consistent with actual progress.

◆ Deployment Checklist

## Three. Our Deployment Checklist

This section proposes questions for deployment preparation. It does not describe a certification engagement or claim certification experience.

1. Which uses belong in scope?  We would ask whether AI drafts text, retrieves documents, or participates in decisions. Write down inputs, output purposes, and recipients. If the answer is “everyone uses it,” start with one describable task.

2. Who may change the rules?  Identify who approves data uploads, model or plugin changes, and who can suspend use. The point is a clear decision owner, not assigning every responsibility to one engineer.

3. What demonstrates routine execution?  Keep tests, versions, incident handling, and improvement tracking under the relevant use. Records should explain decisions made at the time rather than being reconstructed only before an audit.

4. What needs specialist review?  Turn contract, privacy, and sector-specific questions into explicit requests for qualified advisers. This introduction is informational, not legal advice or a conformity assessment.

## Four.  Our Recommendations: Start with One Use and Traceable Records

1. Inventory AI uses.  Record purpose, owner, sources, users, supplier, and shutdown method. Include services actually used, beyond the purchasing list.

2. Connect risks to responses.  For outdated documents, unsupported answers, or unauthorized retrieval, name the reviewer, response, and retest condition. This is our practical application of the risk-management direction in ISO’s public guidance.[3]

3. Keep change and correction records.  When changing a model, document source, or tool, record the change, approval, and test questions. Track incident outcomes and open actions rather than closing a ticket with “improved.”

4. Confirm certification needs separately.  Discuss scope, procedures, and evidence with the certification body when required. ISO describes certification as voluntary, while some industries may have contractual or legal requirements; assess the specific situation.[3][4]

Build everyday management records that an independent reviewer can follow.

◆ Editor’s Note · How Think BIG Approaches This: Responsibility Before Paperwork

## Connect uses, owners, checks, and improvements.

(The following is Think BIG’s practical position, separate from the reporting above.)

We recommend deployment records tied to actual work, with an approval, testing, shutdown, and improvement contact for each use. Governance can expand gradually; a written policy alone does not complete the work.

This is Think BIG’s governance position. It is not a claim that Think BIG holds ISO/IEC 42001 certification.

### Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What does ISO/IEC 42001 cover?
ISO/IEC 42001:2023 covers AI management systems for organizations providing or using AI.[2]
Q2: Is it relevant to users of external AI services?
Yes. ISO’s public description includes organizations using AI systems.[2][3]
Q3: Does ISO issue the certificate?
No. ISO develops standards; external certification bodies perform certification.[4]
Q4: Does certification eliminate answer checks?
We recommend task acceptance checks. Management-system assessment and the accuracy of an individual output are different questions.[2][3]

Sources
    Fact-checked: 2026-10-26.

    [1] UKAS, “AI accreditation update,” September 5, 2025, accessed 2026-10-26: [www.ukas.com](https://www.ukas.com/resources/latest-news/ai-accreditation-update/) ·
    [2] ISO, “ISO/IEC 42001:2023,” public description, accessed 2026-10-26: [www.iso.org](https://www.iso.org/standard/42001) ·
    [3] ISO, “ISO/IEC 42001 explained”, accessed 2026-10-26: [www.iso.org](https://www.iso.org/insights/iso-42001-explained) ·
    [4] ISO, “Certification”, accessed 2026-10-26: [www.iso.org](https://www.iso.org/certification.html)

# Thinking about abandoning your AI Agent? Ask these three questions first | Think BIG NEWS

# THINK BIG

SEEN BY AI

Friday, October 3, 2026
◆
First-hand observations on AI deployment
◆
Issue 001

AI Agent Deployment

## Thinking about abandoning your AI Agent? Ask these three questions first — and stop getting locked in

Think BIG Editorial  |  October 3, 2026

Most AI Agent abandonment has nothing to do with the tool itself. It comes down to three things nobody confirmed at the start: can you switch models, who owns the data, and can you predict the monthly cost? Get these three right upfront, and so-called "abandonment waves" will have nothing to do with you.

(Note: "Lobster" and "Hermes" are informal names used in the Taiwanese tech community for a category of AI Agent tools that can run continuously and operate the computer on your behalf. This article addresses deployment methodology for that type of tool, staying focused on the phenomenon without targeting any specific company or product.)

## 1.  The Situation: What the conversation is really about

AI Agents — AI assistants that can take action and complete tasks on their own — have moved over the past year from early-adopter experiments into real workflows. Alongside that shift came a familiar pattern: install it, use it for two or three weeks, lose interest, leave it gathering digital dust. This "abandonment" isn't unique to Taiwan; the whole industry is grappling with it.

A few independently verifiable observations from published research: industry analysts project that by 2027, more than 40%  of AI Agent projects may be abandoned or cancelled by businesses — and the cause is rarely the technology itself. The most common culprits are unclear governance and unexamined ROI assumptions.

One survey of senior executives found that roughly 80%  of respondents were concerned about "over-reliance on a single AI vendor." Separate reporting notes that after months of accumulated configuration and context, switching AI Agent providers is far from a simple URL swap — and switching costs keep rising.

In short, abandonment usually comes down to two underlying problems: starting without a clear use case, then discovering the tool doesn't fit ; and getting so embedded in a setup that you can't leave even when you want to . Whether the tool itself is good barely enters into it.

## 2.  The Debate: Two legitimate perspectives

The optimistic view  is that the core value of a continuously running AI Agent is precisely that you don't need to supervise it — it lives in your messaging app and on your computer, sends proactive reminders, reports on schedule, and learns your habits. For solo operators and small businesses, that's the equivalent of a tireless assistant who never clocks out.

The skeptical view  centres on three concerns: lock-in risk (model, data, and configuration all tied to one vendor), cost unpredictability (pricing structures vary widely across the market — fixed fee, usage-based, or hybrid — and the difference matters over a year), and maintenance burden (getting it running and keeping it stable are two very different things).

These perspectives don't actually contradict each other. The optimists are talking about the value ; the skeptics are talking about how to deploy without stepping on a landmine . Whether you end up abandoning the tool almost always comes down to whether you addressed those three skeptic concerns before you started.

◆ First-Hand Notes

## 3. What we learned from actually doing this

"Running" doesn't mean "running well."  We deployed a local AI setup on one machine that looked fine — it answered questions — but every single response took one to four minutes, sometimes timing out entirely. After a long diagnostic detour, we found the model had been running entirely on the CPU. The GPU was doing nothing. Now we check GPU utilization before we change anything else.

One verifiable metric is all you need.  For Ollama-based setups, ollama ps  shows the PROCESSOR column (100% GPU, 100% CPU, or a split). The API also returns video RAM usage (size_vram ). If video RAM usage is zero, it's running entirely on CPU  — regardless of how normal things look. We screenshot this number before every delivery.

The reason is usually not "not enough hardware."  Three root causes we've encountered, none of which require buying new equipment: the GPU wasn't detected (some integrated or hybrid graphics cards need extra environment configuration); the install path contained non-ASCII characters that crashed the detection process; the context window was set too large, which exhausted shared system memory and caused repeated crashes across the whole machine. AI memory is not "bigger is always better."

Nobody can promise perfect security.  What we can do is check every layer: scan skills before installation, pin versions, audit again before going live, and keep keys in system config rather than in plain text. This isn't "we're safer than others" — it's "we've checked everything that can be checked."

## 4.  Our recommendation: Three questions to answer before you deploy

Can you switch the underlying model?  Is the tool tied to a single AI provider, or can you swap models freely? An architecture that lets you choose and switch means that when a better or cheaper model appears, you can move. That's the exit you want to have.

Who holds the data?  Does it run on your own hardware, or on someone else's cloud? Local deployment keeps your data under your control. Cloud is also fine — but you should know exactly where your data sits before you commit.

Can you predict the monthly cost?  Fixed fee, or does it scale with usage? A plan where you can estimate costs in advance and stay within budget serves long-term operations far better than one where the bill might surprise you.

One line to close with: abandonment is decided before deployment, not by the tool.  Make sure you can switch models, that your data stays in your control, and that costs are predictable — and an AI Agent stops being a one-time experiment and starts being a genuine long-term collaborator.

◆ Editorial · How Think BIG approaches this

## What this architecture actually delivers

The three questions above are precisely what we lock down at the start of every deployment. The architecture we use delivers three concrete outcomes:

1. No single-model lock-in; API costs stay predictable.  The underlying model is interchangeable — switch to a lower-cost model when saving budget, switch to a higher-capability model when the task demands it. The same assistant can cost dramatically different amounts from month to month, and you control it.

2. Your data stays on your hardware.  Local deployment keeps records and configuration on your machine, not someone else's cloud.

3. Pinned versions, layered security review.  No automatic updates; every skill goes through a security check before going live — stable, maintainable, and auditable.

This is why the so-called "abandonment wave" doesn't touch the people who deploy this way: model flexibility, data ownership, and cost predictability are built in from day one.

### FAQ · Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Is it normal to stop using an AI Agent after a few weeks?
Very common. Industry projections suggest more than 40% of projects may be abandoned by 2027. But in most cases it's not the tool — it's that deployment started without clarifying the problem to solve, or whether the setup could be changed, or what the cost would look like.
Q: How do I know if an AI Agent will lock me in?
Check three things: can you choose and swap the underlying AI model; is the data on your machine or someone else's cloud; is the cost fixed or usage-based. Flexibility on all three keeps lock-in risk low.
Q: Local or cloud — which suits me?
Depends on the use case. If data residency matters, you want continuous operation, or you need predictable costs, local deployment makes more sense. For instant access without managing maintenance, cloud is more convenient. Both can be combined.
Q: What should I watch out for with third-party skills or plugins?
They typically have direct access to your files and accounts. Verify the source, run a basic security check, pin the version, and turn off auto-updates. Nobody can promise perfect security — the goal is to check every layer you can.

     ·
    AI Agent switching costs reporting:
    [itbrew.com](https://www.itbrew.com/stories/ai-agents-vendor-switching)

This article is a Think BIG field notes publication, based on first-hand deployment experience. The views expressed do not represent any specific vendor or product. All named sources are linked inline.

# Choosing a Local AI Model: Bigger Isn't Automatically Better — Test It on Your Own Work | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Local AI Field Notes · Issue 013
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

LOCAL AI FIELD NOTES

October 31, 2026  ·  Saturday
◆
Local AI Field Notes
◆
Issue 013

Local LLM · Model Selection · VRAM Management

## Choosing a Local AI Model: Bigger Isn’t Automatically Better — Test It on Your Own Work

Think BIG Media  |  October 31, 2026

When choosing a local model, ask what work the machine has to do, then whether the model fits, and finally test it on your real tasks. A large model that doesn’t fit in VRAM can run slower than a smaller one that sits entirely on the GPU.

(We use the open-source tool Ollama to illustrate the checks. This article does not rank or recommend any specific model.)
Our Issue 2 asked whether the GPU was doing anything; Issue 11 looked at context lengths set too high. This issue connects the two: the model, the context, and the number of people served at once all draw on the same memory.

## One. What’s Happening: The Model and the Context Compete for Memory

"Can I run the biggest one on my own machine?" is often the first question. Answering it means doing the memory math for everything at once.

Ollama's documentation says a larger context length increases the memory needed to run a model, and that you should confirm you have enough VRAM before raising it. The same page recommends at least 64,000 tokens of context for tasks such as agents and coding tools, and advises avoiding offloading the model to the CPU for best performance.[2] The FAQ adds that when serving several requests at once, required memory scales with parallel requests multiplied by context length.[1]

Put simply, an AI agent already needs a fairly large context. The bigger the model you pick, the less room is left for that context and for concurrent requests.

Quantization is the usual trade-off tool. The documentation describes it as storing model weights at lower precision to reduce the memory needed to load and use a model while preserving as much accuracy as possible. Weights are typically stored as 32-bit or 16-bit floating point, and some methods go further down to integer formats such as int8 or int4.[4]

## Two. Perspectives: Read the Spec Sheet, or Run the Test?

The spec-sheet view:  more parameters and longer context mean more potential. For complex reasoning or very long documents that has merit, and the guidance above does support larger contexts for agent tasks.[2]

The testing view:  The US National Institute of Standards and Technology's AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) says accuracy measurements should be paired with clearly defined, realistic test sets that represent conditions of expected use, along with details of the test method; system performance should be measured and demonstrated under conditions similar to the deployment setting.[5] Ollama's FAQ makes a related point about K/V cache quantization: its effect on answer quality depends on the model and task, and you may need to experiment to find the right balance.[1]

Both views can coexist. Order is what matters: the spec sheet decides which candidates are on the list; testing decides which one you pick.

◆ First-Hand Lessons

## Three. What We've Learned in Practice

These observations come from our local AI agent deployments. They are not industry statistics and don't describe any particular client.

1. "Which model should we install?" is one of the most common questions, and it has no single answer.  The first question is what the machine will mainly do. Answering support emails, summarizing meetings, searching internal documents, and writing code each place different demands on speed, context length, and answer quality.

2. A common sticking point is "it installs, but it can't keep up."  The model loads and answers in chat, but slows down on real work or stalls once two or three people use it at the same time. The cause is often a model that's too large: add the context an agent needs, and memory can't hold it all, so part of the model lands on the CPU. The PROCESSOR column in ollama ps  shows it at a glance.[1]

3. A size down is often enough.  We start with the smallest candidate that passes acceptance, and keep larger models in reserve until real work shows they're needed.

4. Acceptance uses the client's own questions.  Public leaderboards test other people's questions. We ask the owner to prepare a set of questions they actually ask, with reference answers, and compare candidates on that.

## Four. Our Recommendations: Four Steps

1. Write down the tasks and metrics.  List the three to five jobs the machine will do and, for each, the metrics that matter: how many seconds people can wait, how accurate answers must be, whether data can leave the company, and how many people use it at once.

2. Do the memory math: model + context + concurrency.  Check whether the model itself fits in VRAM, then add the context and concurrency the work needs.[1][2] Drop candidates that don't fit, or look at quantized versions.[4]

3. Test on your own questions.  Prepare questions and reference answers that reflect real use, and record how you tested.[5] For speed, the Ollama API response includes eval_count  (output tokens) and eval_duration  (time spent generating output, in nanoseconds); divide one by the other for tokens per second.[3] Check ollama ps  at the same time to confirm PROCESSOR reads 100% GPU.[1]

4. Pick the smallest model that passes.  Among candidates that meet both quality and speed thresholds, choose the smallest. When the work changes, rerun the same test set.

In short: choose a model by measuring it against your work, not by picking the biggest number on the spec sheet.

◆ Editor’s Note · How Think BIG Approaches This: Selections You Can Retest

## Task and metric sheet, acceptance test set, runtime evidence — delivered together.

(The following is Think BIG's own practice, kept separate from the reporting above.)

When we help choose a local model, the deliverable is more than an installed model: a task and metric sheet  — what each job needs and its thresholds, confirmed by the owner; an acceptance test set  — the client's own questions and reference answers, delivered with the test method, so any future model change can be retested the same way; runtime evidence  — the PROCESSOR and CONTEXT columns from ollama ps  plus speed records, as the basis for handover.

Our position: a model choice should be retestable with the same question set.

### Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: Is a model with more parameters always better?
Not necessarily. The model, the context length, and concurrent requests all take memory.[1][2] When a model doesn't fit in VRAM, part of it runs on the CPU and speed can drop noticeably. Test on your own work before deciding.
Q2: How do I know whether a model is running fully on the GPU?
Run ollama ps . PROCESSOR showing 100% GPU means the model is fully loaded on the GPU; 100% CPU or a CPU/GPU split means all or part of it is in system memory.[1]
Q3: Does quantization make a model worse?
Quantization stores weights at lower precision to save memory while trying to preserve accuracy.[4] The actual effect depends on the model and task, and Ollama's documentation suggests experimenting to find the balance.[1] Compare before and after on your own acceptance questions.
Q4: How do I measure a local model's speed?
Ollama's API response includes eval_count  and eval_duration  (in nanoseconds); divide them to get tokens generated per second. load_duration  shows how long the model took to load.[3]
Q5: How should we prepare test questions?
NIST's AI RMF recommends clearly defined, realistic test sets that represent conditions of expected use, with the test method documented.[5] In practice, ask the owner for the questions they really ask, with reference answers.
Q6: How much context does an AI agent need?
Ollama recommends at least 64,000 tokens for agent tasks.[2] That takes a fair amount of memory, so include it when choosing a model; see our Issue 11 for how to set it.

Sources
    Fact-checked on October 24, 2026.

    [2] Ollama, "Context length" (context and memory, recommendation for agent tasks, avoiding CPU offload); accessed October 24, 2026: [docs.ollama.com/context-length](https://docs.ollama.com/context-length)  ·
    [3] Ollama, "Usage" (API response fields eval_count , eval_duration , load_duration ; timings in nanoseconds); accessed October 24, 2026: [docs.ollama.com/api/usage](https://docs.ollama.com/api/usage)  ·
    [4] Hugging Face, "Quantization" (Transformers documentation, overview); accessed October 24, 2026: [huggingface.co](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/quantization/overview)  ·
    [5] NIST, "Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)," NIST AI 100-1, January 26, 2023 (Section 3.1 on accuracy and test sets; MEASURE 2.3): [nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf)

# Is Your Local AI Actually Using the GPU? "Installed" Doesn't Mean "Running Well" | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Field Notes on AI Deployment · Issue 002
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

SEEN BY AI

Monday, October 5, 2026
◆
First-hand observations on AI deployment
◆
Issue 002

Local AI Deployment

## Is your local AI actually using the GPU? "Installed" doesn't mean "running well"

Think BIG Editorial  |  October 5, 2026

When a local AI model is painfully slow — minutes per response, or constant timeouts — the most likely cause isn't underpowered hardware. It's that the model is running entirely on the CPU, and the GPU is sitting idle. One command, ten seconds, and you'll know for certain.

(Note: This article uses Ollama as the illustrative example because it is one of the most common tools for running local models on a personal computer. The underlying principles apply to other runtimes; the specific commands differ.)

## 1.  The Situation: A well-documented gap

Running an AI model on your own machine — no subscription, no data leaving the building, available offline — has gone from an enthusiast experiment to a realistic option for individuals and small teams. The most common complaint that followed is a single sentence: "I installed it, but it's too slow to use."

The open-source community has documented this thoroughly. Ollama's GitHub issue tracker includes reports of models that "occasionally fall back to CPU, causing 100% CPU utilization, until a restart." ([ollama/ollama #13765](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13765)) Another thread describes a version update that caused models to stop using the GPU entirely. ([ollama/ollama #13320](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13320)) Published troubleshooting guides note that this failure mode is particularly insidious because it produces no error message  — an outdated driver, a disabled environment variable, and the model quietly falls back to CPU, while everything on screen looks normal. ([cmaven.github.io](https://cmaven.github.io/en/etc/ollama-multi-gpu-troubleshooting/), [localaimaster.com](https://localaimaster.com/blog/ollama-not-using-gpu))

In other words: a "slow local AI" is usually not a performance problem. It's a configuration problem that hasn't been noticed yet.

## 2.  The Debate: Is local deployment worth it?

The case for local deployment  is concrete: data stays on your hardware, there's no per-token bill anxiety, and the model can run around the clock as part of an AI Agent workflow. For anyone who cares about privacy or wants continuous AI presence without ongoing cloud costs, this is something cloud services simply can't offer.

The reservations  cluster around two points:

The setup threshold is higher than expected.  Driver version, environment variables, model size relative to video RAM, memory allocation — any one of these being wrong degrades the result significantly, and there's no obvious starting point for diagnosis.

Hardware has to match the model.  If the model is larger than the available video RAM, the overflow gets offloaded to the CPU. The official Ollama FAQ notes that models can end up in a "partial CPU, partial GPU" state. ([docs.ollama.com/faq](https://docs.ollama.com/faq)) That split slows everything down.

Both sides are pointing at the same thing: local AI can be excellent, but only after someone confirms it's actually running on the right hardware.

◆ First-Hand Notes

## 3. What we learned from actually doing this

"Looks fine" is the most dangerous state.  We had a machine where the model was installed, conversations worked, and nothing reported an error — but every response took one to four minutes, with occasional timeouts. We spent considerable time adjusting other settings before finally checking: the model had been running 100% on the CPU. The GPU was untouched. We now check GPU utilization before touching anything else.

One metric is all you need.  ollama ps  shows the PROCESSOR column — 100% GPU, 100% CPU, or a split. The API also returns video RAM usage (size_vram ). If size_vram  is zero, the model is on CPU,  regardless of what everything else looks like. We screenshot this number before every delivery.

Three root causes we've actually encountered  — none requiring a hardware upgrade:

The GPU wasn't detected.  Some newer integrated or hybrid graphics architectures aren't automatically recognized. They require additional environment configuration, and that configuration must be set for the specific user account that runs the model, not just the admin account.

The install path contained non-ASCII characters.  The detection process crashed silently when the path included characters outside standard ASCII. Moving to a plain ASCII path fixed it immediately — the kind of trap that never appears in any spec sheet.

The context window was set too large.  Setting the AI's memory (context window) too high exhausted shared system RAM and caused cascading system instability. Ollama defaults to 4096 tokens (per the official FAQ) — that's a reasonable baseline. Increasing it is fine, but it should be sized to the machine.

The difference after fixing it.  Same machine, same model — switching from CPU-only to actual GPU use took response time from "minutes per question" to "output starts within seconds." That's a configuration fix, not a hardware upgrade.

## 4.  Our recommendation: Three steps when local AI is slow

Check the PROCESSOR column first — before anything else.  Run ollama ps . 100% CPU means the GPU isn't being used; a CPU/GPU split usually means the model is larger than available video RAM. This takes ten seconds and can save hours.

Match model size to video RAM.  Bigger isn't always better. A smaller model that fits entirely in video RAM will often outperform a larger model that spills onto the CPU. Choose based on what your hardware can actually hold.

Make "confirm the GPU" a standing check.  Driver updates, software updates, and account changes can all silently revert to CPU. Check after any meaningful change — don't wait for "why is this slow again?" to surface the issue.

One line to close with: when local AI is slow, suspect the configuration before the hardware.  In most cases, the machine is capable enough — it just hasn't been used correctly yet.

◆ Editorial · How Think BIG approaches this

## What "delivered and running well" actually means

When we deploy a local AI Agent on a client's machine, "GPU actually running" is a mandatory pre-delivery check — not something we do only when a problem surfaces. Our delivery standard includes:

Evidence before handoff, not a verbal "it's installed."  We confirm which hardware the model is using and record the video RAM consumption. We also run a task that calls a tool — not just a chat response — and verify the response time. Screenshots are kept as delivery documentation.

Your data stays on your hardware.  Local deployment keeps records and configuration on your machine. The model can be swapped as better or lower-cost options emerge.

Pinned versions; no automatic updates.  A version update is one of the most common causes of GPU fallback. We pin the version and validate any update before applying it — stability over chasing the latest release.

The value of local AI only materializes once it's confirmed to be running on the right hardware. That confirmation is what we deliver before handing over the keys.

### FAQ · Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How do I check whether my local AI model is using the GPU?
For Ollama, run ollama ps  and look at the PROCESSOR column. 100% GPU means fully on GPU; 100% CPU means the GPU is not being used; a split ratio means only part of the model fits in video RAM.
Q: I have a dedicated GPU — why is the AI still running on CPU?
Common causes: outdated driver, an environment variable that has disabled GPU access, a model larger than available video RAM, or the GPU not detected by the software. Most of these produce no error message, so you have to check actively.
Q: My local AI takes minutes per response. Is my hardware too weak?
Not necessarily. In most cases we've investigated, the model was running entirely on CPU. Confirm GPU is being used before deciding to upgrade.
Q: Is a bigger model always better?
No. A model that doesn't fit in video RAM has part offloaded to CPU, which can make it slower than a smaller model that fits entirely on the GPU. Match model size to available video RAM.
Q: How large should I set the context window?
Ollama defaults to 4096 tokens. Increasing is fine, but each step up consumes more RAM; setting it too high can destabilize the whole machine. Increase gradually based on your hardware, not all at once.

Sources

    [docs.ollama.com](https://docs.ollama.com/faq)
     ·
    Ollama GitHub #13765 (intermittent CPU fallback):
    [github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13765](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13765)
     ·
    Ollama GitHub #13320 (update breaks GPU use):
    [github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13320](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/issues/13320)
     ·
    Multi-GPU troubleshooting guide (driver version, silent CPU fallback):
    [cmaven.github.io](https://cmaven.github.io/en/etc/ollama-multi-gpu-troubleshooting/)
     ·

    [localaimaster.com](https://localaimaster.com/blog/ollama-not-using-gpu)

# Why Do Some Companies Run AI Agents on Their Own Machines Instead of the Cloud? Start With One Question: Can the Data Leave? | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Field Notes · Issue 008
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

AI DEPLOYMENT FIELD NOTES

Monday, October 19, 2026
◆
First-hand AI deployment notes
◆
Issue 008

On-Premises vs. Cloud · AI Agent Deployment · Data Security

## Why Do Some Companies Run AI Agents on Their Own Machines Instead of the Cloud? Start With One Question: Can the Data Leave?

Think BIG Content Team  |  October 19, 2026

Companies keep AI agents on their own machines mostly because the data can't leave the building. On-premises, the model and documents are processed on company hardware. The cloud is faster to launch and needs no hardware, but your questions and document excerpts go to the model provider. Neither is better; it depends on the job.

## 1.  What's happening: "Can this data leave?" is now the first question in any AI rollout

There's one key difference between a chatbot and an AI agent: an AI agent goes and gets data on its own and takes action on its own.  It might read your price quotes, dig through support tickets, check inventory, then turn the results into a reply or write them into a system. It touches far more data than the few lines a person types into a chat window.

So when companies evaluate AI agents, the first question often isn't "Which model is smartest?" It's "Is it OK for this data to leave the company? "

Taiwan's public sector has already answered that question once. The Reference Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI by the Executive Yuan and Its Agencies , drafted by the National Science and Technology Council and presented to the Executive Yuan on August 31, 2023 before being issued to agencies, say in point four that staff must not give generative AI any information that is confidential, personal, or not yet approved for release, and must not ask it questions that could involve confidential matters or personal data. Then comes the exception: a generative AI model deployed in a closed, on-premises environment may be used according to classification level, once the security of the system environment has been confirmed.  (Source: [Executive Yuan press release, 2023-08-31](https://www.ey.gov.tw/Page/9277F759E41CCD91/e63572a7-fb79-4c02-9ea3-b731e7c06a56))

In other words, under the public sector's rules, the same generative AI gets treated two different ways depending on whether it's processed outside or inside your own environment.

Private companies aren't bound by that guideline, but they have their own concerns. Article 21 of Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act lets the competent authority restrict a private organization's international transfer of personal data in certain cases, such as when major national interests are involved or the receiving country lacks adequate data protection laws. (Source: [Laws & Regulations Database, Personal Data Protection Act, Article 21](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawSingle.aspx?pcode=I0050021&flno=21)) Confidentiality clauses in client contracts and industry regulators' rules can also shape where data is allowed to go.

Meanwhile, running models on your own computer keeps getting easier. Open-source tools for local models are now common, and the official FAQ of one popular tool puts it plainly: when you run locally, the developer doesn't see your prompts or data, but if you switch to its cloud-hosted models, your prompts and responses are processed by its service. (Source: [Ollama official FAQ](https://docs.ollama.com/faq)) Same tool, different mode, completely different data flow.

In short: the difference between on-premises and cloud isn't about which technology is newer. It's about where the data goes.

## 2.  The debate: what the cloud camp and the on-prem camp each get right

The cloud camp's  case is practical: you're up and running fast, with no machines to buy and no GPUs to manage, and the newest, most capable models usually show up in the cloud first. For teams whose data isn't very sensitive and who want to try things out, the cloud is the easiest place to start.

Cloud providers are also responding to data concerns. Take one major AI model provider's enterprise privacy page: business data isn't used to train its models by default, and API inputs and outputs may be retained for up to 30 days to provide the service and detect abuse, then deleted, with zero data retention available for qualifying use cases. (Source: [OpenAI Enterprise Privacy](https://openai.com/enterprise-privacy/)) The terms are getting clearer, and that's a fact.

The on-prem camp  looks at the other side: no matter how clear the terms are, the data still left the company, and you're relying on the other party to keep its promises and on its systems not to fail. On-premises, the model and documents are processed on company hardware, and questions never pass through an outside model provider. Costs are mostly equipment, so they don't swing month to month with usage.

On-premises comes with clear costs too: someone has to look after it  (the machine has to stay on 24/7, and somebody has to deal with power outages, reboots, and full disks); hardware caps model capability  (the models a company machine can run are usually smaller than the largest cloud models); upgrades are your call  (cloud providers upgrade models for you; on-premises, you evaluate, test, and switch versions yourself).

Both sides are right. The real question isn't "which side?" It's which side each type of data in your company belongs on.

◆ First-hand notes

## 3. What we've learned doing this work

Think BIG deploys AI agents for businesses both on-premises and in the cloud. Here's what we've learned, with no client details:

1. Map the data flow before choosing on-prem or cloud.  Before we start, we list where six things will live: the application, the model, the knowledge base index, the original documents, conversation logs, and backups. Many people assume "installed locally" means everything is local. But the moment you connect an outside chat channel like LINE, messages sent through that channel pass through that service. All of this has to be spelled out before rollout.

2. "Local" doesn't mean "never connects out."  Automatic updates, error reporting, and remote maintenance connections can all make a machine reach the internet. Keeping data from leaving takes more than a local model; you also have to check logs, backups, and every outside integration.

3. With dual-mode tools, confirm which mode you're actually using.  As noted above, some local model tools also offer cloud models. We confirm that the model in use really is local and turn off cloud features when needed, so nobody ends up thinking data stays local when it's actually being sent out.

4. The most common on-prem trap: "it installs" doesn't mean "it runs well."  If the model never touches the GPU and runs entirely on the CPU, answers get so slow that nobody wants to use it. We covered this in [Think BIG NEWS No. 2](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/local-llm-gpu-check-20261005/). Acceptance has to rest on measured results, not on how smooth the demo looks.

5. The most underestimated cloud cost: how much an AI agent uses.  Chat is one question, one answer. To finish a single task, an AI agent often calls the model several times, and usage multiplies. Cloud billing is mostly usage-based, so estimate before rollout and set usage caps and alerts.

6. On-prem or cloud, accounts belong in the company's name.  Cloud API access is set up under the company's own account, so the company confirms terms directly with the model provider. On-premises, the machines, data, and configuration all belong to the company too. That way, switching models or vendors later never leaves you locked in.

Our biggest takeaway: on-prem versus cloud isn't a matter of belief. It's a matter of data classification.  Sort your data first, and the answer usually becomes obvious.

## 4.  Our recommendations: three questions that decide where it goes

1. Can this type of data leave the company?  Check three things: confidentiality clauses in client contracts, your industry regulator's rules, and whether personal data is involved. If any one of them says no, that data belongs on-premises. 2. How much will it be used, and will that grow?  If a few people ask occasional questions, the cloud is a bargain. If the whole company uses it every day and AI agents run workflows automatically, factor monthly usage into the comparison. 3. Is anyone available to look after a machine?  On-premises needs someone, internal or external, to keep it running, monitor it, and update it. Without that, even a great on-prem system slowly breaks down.

On-premises Cloud Hybrid
Data flow Model and documents processed on company hardware Questions and document excerpts sent to the model provider Sensitive data on-prem, general data in the cloud

Best for Companies with lots of contracts, personal data, or internal secrets Teams that want to try fast with low-sensitivity data Companies with both kinds of data and a clear way to tell them apart

Main cost Equipment and maintenance Usage-based billing Both, plus two systems to manage

Watch out for Needs someone to maintain it; hardware caps model capability Terms and model versions change Data classification has to come first

Bottom line: ask whether the data can leave before you decide where your AI agent lives.

◆ Editor's Note · How Think BIG Approaches This

## On-premises by default. Security reviewed before every launch.

(The following reflects Think BIG's own position and is separate from the neutral reporting above.)

We start from protecting our clients' security and build AI agents on the company's own machines. All three plans offer two deployment options: On-premises edition  — the model and documents are processed on your company's machines, and questions don't pass through an outside model provider. If you add outside channels such as LINE, messages through those channels pass through that service; we list every item for you before rollout. Cloud-assisted edition  — model API access is set up under your company's own account. Questions and retrieved document excerpts are sent to the model provider for processing, under that provider's terms of service. It suits companies whose data policies allow it, that want to launch fast, and that don't want to manage hardware.

Security review before every launch:  every launch goes through a security review of code and configuration first, and nothing ships until it passes. Third-party packages are version-pinned, keys stay out of version control, and cloud accounts are opened in your company's name. Delivery within 30 days:  delivery happens within 30 days once scope is frozen and the data is in place, with the first year of maintenance included.

Nobody can promise perfect security. What we do is review it, step by step.

### FAQ

Q1: Why do some companies run AI agents on their own computers?
The most common reason is that their data can't or shouldn't leave the company: client contracts have confidentiality clauses, the data includes personal information, or an industry regulator has rules. On-premises deployment keeps the model and documents on company hardware, so questions never pass through an outside model provider.
Q2: What's the difference between running an AI agent on-premises and in the cloud?
Where the data goes. On-premises, it's processed on the company's own hardware; in the cloud, questions and relevant document excerpts are sent to the model provider. The cloud launches faster and needs no hardware; on-premises needs ongoing maintenance, and hardware limits model capability.
Q3: If it's installed locally, does that mean the data never leaves?
Not necessarily. Automatic updates, error reporting, remote maintenance, or a connection to an outside chat channel like LINE can all route data through outside services. Keeping data in-house takes more than a local model; you also need to check logs, backups, and every outside integration.
Q4: Can Taiwan's government agencies use on-premises generative AI for confidential data?
Under point four of the Reference Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI by the Executive Yuan and Its Agencies, a generative AI model deployed in a closed, on-premises environment may be used according to classification level once the security of the system environment has been confirmed. Each agency's own rules still govern actual practice.
Q5: Should a small business choose on-premises or cloud?
Ask three questions first: can the data leave the company, how heavy will usage be, and is anyone available to look after a machine? Sensitive data points to on-premises; a quick trial with low-sensitivity data can start in the cloud. If you have both kinds of data, a hybrid setup works, but classify your data first.

Sources
    Executive Yuan press release on the Reference Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI  (2023-08-31; includes the NSTC press release and full guideline text, with the closed on-premises exception in point four): [ey.gov.tw](https://www.ey.gov.tw/Page/9277F759E41CCD91/e63572a7-fb79-4c02-9ea3-b731e7c06a56)  ·
    Laws & Regulations Database of the Republic of China (Taiwan), Personal Data Protection Act, Article 21: [law.moj.gov.tw](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawSingle.aspx?pcode=I0050021&flno=21)  ·
    Ollama official FAQ: [docs.ollama.com](https://docs.ollama.com/faq)  ·
    OpenAI, "Enterprise Privacy": [openai.com](https://openai.com/enterprise-privacy/)  ·

# What Is MCP? Set Permission Boundaries Before Connecting an AI Agent | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Enterprise Security Notes · Issue 014
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

ENTERPRISE SECURITY NOTES

November 2, 2026  ·  Monday
◆
Enterprise Security Notes
◆
Issue 014

MCP · AI Agents · Access Control

## What Is MCP? Set Permission Boundaries Before Connecting an AI Agent

Think BIG Media  |  November 2, 2026

Before connecting an agent, define what it may read, change, and send. Review the connection protocol, authentication, and business approvals separately.

## One.  What’s Happening: Connections Are Easier; Accountability Stays with the Business

In May 2025, Anthropic announced an API MCP connector that let developers connect to remote MCP servers without writing separate client code.[1] That announcement is the starting point for this practical discussion, rather than a new product update. Easier connections shift the business question from whether an agent can connect to what it may do afterward.

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. Its tools specification lets servers expose functions a model can invoke, including database queries, API calls, and computations.[3] Reading a list and editing it remain different business actions even when both appear in the same tool menu. We recommend assigning approval conditions to each action.

The authorization document at the 2025-06-18 path covers HTTP transports and says STDIO implementations should obtain credentials from the environment instead.[2] The tools document requires server access controls and recommends user confirmation for sensitive operations.[3] A successful connection therefore does not complete permission acceptance.

## Two.  Perspectives: Interoperability Helps; Authorization Still Needs Work

The case for adoption:  The connector announcement describes less custom client work for remote integrations.[1] In our assessment, a consistent interface can also help teams inventory tools. It does not make each connected system’s data boundaries or business responsibilities identical.

The caution:  The authorization specification requires servers to validate that access tokens were issued for them.[2] The security guidance describes how insufficiently restricted local MCP programs can execute commands, expose data, or cause data loss.[4] These are implementation risks, not a claim that every MCP service has suffered an incident.

We recommend separate records for connectivity, permissions, and approvals. Engineering maps the data flow. The system owner defines accessible fields. The business owner identifies changes that require a person to approve them. Being signed in should not serve as permission for every available action.

Consider a hypothetical permission test: someone may read a document, but may they ask the agent to email it externally? If the answers differ, document separate conditions for reading and sending. The approval view should identify the actual document and recipient, with consent scoped to this action.

For cross-system work, map revocation responsibilities. Disabling the AI tool, disconnecting MCP, and revoking a downstream account are different control points; the required combination depends on the architecture. Ask the maintainer to demonstrate shutdown and test the result. Track unfinished work before deciding how to close it.

We also recommend acceptance with a restricted test identity, beyond an administrator’s successful demonstration. Run both permitted and denied actions and have the owner review the reasons. This establishes a usable baseline for future access changes.

◆ First-Hand Lessons

## Three. What We Learned in Practice

These points come from our review practice for skills, plugins, and MCP servers. They are not industry statistics or an account of any particular organization.

1. Read what the program actually does.  We check its source, maintainer, license, access to environment variables or keys, outbound connections, and execution of downloaded code. A tool labeled “search” still needs a review of its actual operations.

2. Review permissions and versions together.  We check requested privileges and pin versions. Packages that fail review are not installed. This creates a traceable decision before introducing third-party code; it does not remove all risk.

3. Record unresolved questions.  Extending that practice, we recommend tracking unexplained destinations, write operations, and credential sources. A program starting successfully is not a reason to close the review.

## Four.  Our Recommendations: Turn Boundaries into Repeatable Tests

1. Inventory tools.  Record the system, account, folders or tables, read and write capabilities, and owner. Start query tools with read-only accounts. Document the reason and approver for any write access.

2. Enforce restrictions in the system.  Use account permissions, API authorization, or server rules, then test that out-of-scope requests are rejected. Prompts can explain a policy; acceptance should demonstrate its enforcement.[3]

3. Preview sensitive operations.  We recommend human confirmation before sending messages, deleting records, or changing production data. Show the recipient, target, and proposed change. This turns the specification’s confirmation guidance into a usable workflow.[3]

4. Test revocation and record results.  With test data, check permitted access, denied access, and failure after revocation. Record time, actor, and outcome without logging full credentials. Set tool-call timeouts too.[2][3]

Demonstrate permission boundaries with rejection tests and approval records.

◆ Editor’s Note · How Think BIG Approaches This: Connections You Can Revoke

## Deliver the tool inventory, approval conditions, and revocation tests together.

(The following is Think BIG’s practical position, separate from the reporting above.)

Our position is that every integration should have a documented purpose, data scope, and maintenance contact. Human confirmation for sensitive operations belongs in acceptance. Review the changed components whenever a tool or permission is added.

The handover should let the owner understand the authorization and stop the connection.

### Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: Is MCP an AI model?
No. Its tools specification describes how models invoke external functions.[3]
Q2: Does MCP handle all permissions?
Access controls still need implementation in the server and connected systems.[2][3]
Q3: Should local MCP programs be reviewed?
Yes. The security guidance identifies local command execution and data access risks.[4]
Q4: What should require approval?
We recommend previews and designated approvers for messages, deletions, and production changes, applying the sensitive-operation guidance.[3]

Sources
    Fact-checked: 2026-10-26.

    [1] Anthropic, “New capabilities for building agents on the Anthropic API,” May 22, 2025, accessed 2026-10-26: [www.anthropic.com](https://www.anthropic.com/news/agent-capabilities-api) ·
    [2] MCP, “Authorization,” 2025-06-18 path, accessed 2026-10-26: [modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/authorization) ·
    [3] MCP, “Tools,” 2025-06-18 path, accessed 2026-10-26: [modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools) ·
    [4] MCP, “Security Best Practices”, accessed 2026-10-26: [modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices)

# Can a Chinese Windows Username Disrupt Local AI? Check Paths and Logs | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Local AI Field Notes · Issue 015
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

LOCAL AI FIELD NOTES

November 4, 2026  ·  Wednesday
◆
Local AI Field Notes
◆
Issue 015

Windows · Unicode Paths · Local AI

## Can a Chinese Windows Username Disrupt Local AI? Check Paths and Logs

Think BIG Media  |  November 4, 2026

A Chinese username is not a configuration error. When installation or GPU discovery fails, inspect the path the tool receives before changing directories.

## One.  What’s Happening: Unicode Support Does Not Validate Every Component

A local model running on the CPU can have a problem outside the model itself. Microsoft documents Unicode storage for long filenames and distinguishes ANSI code-page APIs from Unicode APIs.[1][2] A valid Chinese path in Windows does not establish that every package, subprocess, or startup script passes it correctly. That is a diagnostic possibility, not a diagnosis based on someone’s username.

Ollama’s troubleshooting guide recommends inspecting logs and lists Windows log and binary locations.[3] We use that documentation to illustrate an inspection method, without ranking tools or claiming this tool fails on all Chinese accounts.

Our deployment record was specific: the model answered, but used the CPU. Debug logs showed GPU-discovery subprocess failures and corrupted paths. That internal record supports the practice notes below. It cannot tell us how often this happens on other computers.

## Two.  Perspectives: Support Valid Names and Keep Deployment Paths Maintainable

The user perspective:  Chinese names and file paths are legitimate needs, consistent with Microsoft’s Unicode documentation.[1][2] We believe a reproducible tool failure should be documented for maintainers rather than attributed to the user’s choice of name.

The operations perspective:  A simple English program directory can help isolate a variable in a particular environment. This is our deployment trade-off, not a general Windows requirement. Keep the model, tool version, and driver unchanged where possible when comparing paths.

Microsoft documents mklink /j  as creating a Directory Junction.[4] A junction does not repair a tool’s text encoding. Whether to use one, and which way it should point, depends on the file layout and startup method. A single command is not a universal fix.

Use a comparison table: tool and model, startup directory, execution account, and failing step. Changing several variables together makes attribution difficult. If they must change together, say so rather than crediting the entire result to an English path.

If the English-directory test does not help, return to the logs and investigate other causes. Avoid further bulk moves or rebuilding every account because of this case. Preserve unsuccessful tests too so another maintainer can continue.

◆ First-Hand Lessons

## Three. What We Learned in Practice

These observations come from one Windows deployment and maintenance record. They are not industry statistics and do not identify any particular organization.

1. It initially looked like a GPU issue.  The program and model were under a user directory containing Chinese characters. The model ran slowly on the CPU. Changes to several GPU-related environment variables did not resolve it.

2. Logs pointed toward the path.  Debug records showed all GPU-discovery subprocesses failing and paths appearing as corrupted text. An OpenSSH startup script on the same machine also mishandled the account path. This does not establish a limitation across remote-access tools.

3. We changed program locations while preserving user data.  We moved the program and model to an English directory, connected the old location through a junction, created an English-named management account, and used Task Scheduler for startup. The model then ran fully on the GPU and became visibly faster. We have no measured multiplier to report.

4. We moved the check earlier.  We now inspect the account name with whoami  and plan an English program path when it contains non-ASCII characters. This is a deployment habit, not a request for people to change their names.

## Four.  Our Recommendations: Keep Evidence Before and After Changes

1. Record the environment.  Save the tool version, program and model directories, startup account, and failure time. Record the display name and actual logged path separately. Remove names and tokens before seeking outside support.

2. Read logs before choosing a fix.  Locate logs using the tool documentation and check whether subprocess failures coincide with corrupted paths.[3] Without that evidence, keep driver, permission, and other causes open.

3. Test a copy in another path.  Use a backup or test environment to compare an English directory. Document service, schedule, and model-path changes. If a junction is used, verify its source and target and document rollback.[4]

4. Repeat the original task.  With the same model and question, compare the execution device and errors, then check service startup after reboot. Acceptance should establish that the original failure is gone, beyond simply opening the application.

Let logs guide the investigation and controlled comparisons guide the change.

◆ Editor’s Note · How Think BIG Approaches This: Document the Paths

## Give the next maintainer a usable map of the installation.

(The following is Think BIG’s practical position, separate from the reporting above.)

We recommend documenting physical directories, links, startup accounts, and schedules together. Every change should have a reversal plan; do not casually move an entire user profile.

Path checks and execution-device checks belong in the same acceptance checklist.

### Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: Can a Chinese Windows account run local AI?
Windows supports Unicode. This article describes a specific toolchain problem, not a general prohibition.[1][2]
Q2: Does CPU-only execution prove a path problem?
No. Inspect logs and run controlled comparisons rather than diagnosing from speed or a username.[3]
Q3: What is a junction?
Microsoft documents mklink /j as creating a Directory Junction. It is not an encoding repair.[4]
Q4: Should I rename the whole user profile?
We do not recommend casually moving a whole profile. In this deployment we changed program and model locations while preserving user data.

Sources
    Fact-checked: 2026-10-26.

    [1] Microsoft, “Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces”, accessed 2026-10-26: [learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/naming-a-file) ·
    [2] Microsoft, “Unicode in the Windows API”, accessed 2026-10-26: [learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/intl/unicode-in-the-windows-api) ·
    [3] Ollama, “Troubleshooting”, accessed 2026-10-26: [docs.ollama.com](https://docs.ollama.com/troubleshooting) ·
    [4] Microsoft, “mklink”, accessed 2026-10-26: [learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/mklink)
