# AI Joins the Bug Hunt, and the Patch Window Shrinks — What PHP2Shell Means for Enterprise IT | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Enterprise Security Notes · Issue 012
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

ENTERPRISE SECURITY NOTES

October 29, 2026  ·  Thursday
◆
Enterprise Security Notes
◆
Issue 012

PHP2Shell · Enterprise Security · Patch Management

## AI Joins the Bug Hunt, and the Patch Window Shrinks — What PHP2Shell Means for Enterprise IT

Think BIG Media  |  October 29, 2026

PHP fixed two critical flaws on October 21 that could let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a server. The first job is straightforward: find every system running PHP, move it to a fixed release, and confirm the update took effect.

Our Issue 10, "AI Is Being Used to Automate Attacks," covered the attacker's side: AI speeding up existing attack workflows. This issue covers the defender's side. The same kind of tools are helping find bugs, reports are piling up, patches are arriving faster, and patch processes need to keep pace.

## One. What Happened: Two Critical Flaws Affecting Every Web-Facing PHP Install

On October 21, 2026 , the PHP project released 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 to fix two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution , and urged all PHP users to update immediately.[1] Both are rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0.[2][6][7]

According to the advisory, every PHP installation that serves web requests is at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. PHP rates mod_php as highest risk, with a demonstrated exploit in which an unauthenticated request triggers the attack before any application code runs.[1]

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued an alert the same day, referring to the vulnerabilities as "php2shell." It urged organizations to patch immediately, starting with internet-facing systems, and said that systems which cannot be updated right away, or which still run unsupported PHP 8.1 or earlier, should be taken offline until patched.[4] CISA also noted that PHP is often a component of other software, so where it runs may not be obvious.[4]

On October 23, PHP published a follow-up: under an unusual combination of configuration and application code, a low-likelihood remote execution path remains. It is tracked as CVE-2026-115560, with a full advisory due alongside the next regular bugfix release. Until then, PHP recommends setting session.upload_progress.enabled  to 0.[3]

## Two. Perspectives: AI Brings More Reports, but People Still Make the Calls

The PHP Foundation: tools find bugs faster, for both sides.

In a post published on release day, the PHP Foundation explained that early signs of the root cause surfaced in 2024 during follow-up work on an external audit, and that several outside research groups later reported its full impact.[8] The Foundation also said AI-assisted research has sharply increased the volume of reports: the team has published 15 CVEs since July 1 and worked through more than 100 reports that proved invalid, duplicate, or not reproducible. AI helps validate reports and group those that share a root cause, but a person makes every call and works on every patch.[8] In the Foundation's words, tools now find bugs faster than ever, for defenders and attackers alike.[8]

PHP: the disclosure schedule was pulled forward.

The Foundation explained that around 15:00 UTC on October 20, the two CVE IDs began circulating on forums and social media, along with a wrong release time and a wrong score of 10.0. No technical details leaked. PHP brought its pre-announcement forward and moved the release up a day, from October 22 to October 21 at 14:00 UTC.[8]

CISA: patch now, or take it offline.

CISA's alert says it had not observed successful exploitation as of publication, but unpatched systems remain at risk; a web application firewall may provide some protection until updates are applied.[4] When we checked CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on October 24 (catalog version 2026.10.23), neither CVE was listed.[5] Our reading: not being listed means CISA hasn't added it, not that nobody has been attacked.

Bugs are being found and made public faster. Patching has to speed up to match.

◆ First-Hand Lessons

## Three. What We've Learned in Practice

These observations come from our work on systems and AI tool deployments. They are not industry statistics and don't describe any particular client.

1. "AI found the bug, so who fixes it?" is a common question.  Finding and fixing are different jobs. Someone has to schedule the patch, restart services, and confirm the site still works. AI can help organize that work, but the responsibility has to sit with a named person.

2. "We don't use PHP" is often wrong.  PHP commonly sits inside a website's admin panel, a form plugin, or the management screen of an internal system, and the owner doesn't know it. It's the same point CISA makes about PHP being a component of other software.[4]

3. Check the full package version.  PHP says Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance and that you should check with your vendor for updated packages.[1] A situation we see often: a distribution backports fixes into an older version line, so reading just the first three digits can mislead you. Verify against the full version listed in the vendor's notice.

4. Restart every worker after a configuration change.  PHP's interim guidance says settings such as session.upload_progress.enabled=0  must apply before request parsing, require restarting every worker, and can't rely on ini_set()  in code.[1] We list "recheck version and settings after restart" as an acceptance item.

## Four. Our Recommendations: Three Things First

1. Inventory every place PHP runs.  Include public websites, internal systems, and PHP bundled inside plugins and packages. For each, record the execution mode (FPM, mod_php, and so on), full version, package source, and owner. Internet-facing systems go first.[4]

2. Update to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35.  If you use distribution packages, confirm the corresponding fixed version with your vendor.[1] PHP no longer ships updates for 8.1 and older, so look for a vendor backport or move to a supported version;[1] CISA advises taking systems offline if they can't be dealt with yet.[4] The interim measures PHP lists reduce exposure to specific paths but do not make an installation safe.[1]

3. Write event-driven patching into your process.  Agree in advance who assesses a critical advisory, who approves downtime, how quickly it must be done, and how the fix is verified. Waiting for next month's maintenance window may be too late. Also keep an eye on CVE-2026-115560, due to be addressed in PHP's next regular release.[3]

CISA also recommends monitoring for suspicious activity, such as PHP worker processes launching shells or downloading tools.[4] If you suspect a compromise, preserve logs and hand the matter to authorized responders.

◆ Editor's Note · How Think BIG Approaches This: Make Patching Verifiable

## Inventory sheet, acceptance evidence, emergency patch agreement — built into every deployment.

(The following is Think BIG's own practice, kept separate from the reporting above.)

When we deploy AI agents and the systems around them, the patch process ships with the deployment: an inventory sheet  — site, runtime, package source, full version, owner, maintenance window, and backup and recovery method; acceptance evidence  — version and configuration checks captured after updating and restarting, handed to the owner; an emergency patch agreement  — contacts, approvers, and order of actions for critical advisories, documented in advance.

Our position: AI can help find problems and organize information, but decisions about patching, and responsibility for them, have to sit clearly with people.

### Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What is PHP2Shell?
It's CISA's name for two critical PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both of which can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.[4][1]
Q2: Which versions need updating, and to what?
The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, and every installation serving web requests is in scope.[1] If you use operating-system packages, confirm the matching version with your vendor.[1]
Q3: What if we're still on PHP 8.1 or older?
PHP no longer updates 8.1 and earlier; some distributions and LTS vendors provide backports, so contact your vendor or upgrade.[1] CISA advises taking systems offline if they can't be updated right away.[4]
Q4: Has anyone been attacked yet?
CISA had not observed successful exploitation when its alert was published.[4] When we checked the KEV catalog on October 24 (version 2026.10.23), neither CVE was listed.[5] That doesn't mean there's no risk; patch promptly.
Q5: Is there a workaround if we can't update right now?
PHP lists settings that reduce exposure to specific attack paths, but states plainly that only an update is a complete solution and that these measures don't make an installation safe.[1] CISA notes a WAF may offer some protection in the meantime.[4]
Q6: What role did AI play here?
The PHP Foundation says AI-assisted research has driven a large increase in reports, and AI is also used to validate reports and group those with a shared root cause, while people make every decision and write every patch.[8] Our Issue 10 covered how attackers use AI; this issue covers the defense.

# Should AI Tools Update Automatically? Pin Versions and Plan Patches | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Local AI Field Notes · Issue 017
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

LOCAL AI FIELD NOTES

November 8, 2026  ·  Sunday
◆
Local AI Field Notes
◆
Issue 017

Version Management · AI Agents · Update Acceptance

## Should AI Tools Update Automatically? Pin Versions and Plan Patches

Think BIG Media  |  November 8, 2026

A business AI agent needs a known runtime. Pin a reproducible combination, then assign owners for updates, acceptance checks, and recovery.

## One.  What’s Happening: Repeatability and Patching Belong Together

Updates involve more than new features. pip documents version pinning as a way to build repeatable environments, with hashes available to check downloaded packages.[1] npm’s npm ci  requires an existing lockfile and fails if it conflicts with the package declaration rather than rewriting it.[2] Both make the intended installation more explicit.

NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4, its 2022 enterprise patch-management planning guide, describes identifying, prioritizing, acquiring, installing, and verifying updates.[4] Pinning is therefore no reason to ignore vulnerabilities indefinitely. We recommend recording both the current version combination and the next update review.

Installation methods matter too. Ollama’s Windows documentation distinguishes its installer from a standalone CLI archive that can be integrated as a service.[3] This illustrates why deployment methods should be recorded; it is not a product recommendation or a claim that all AI tools update alike.

## Two.  Perspectives: Automation Helps; Production Changes Need Control

The case for automation:  NIST frames patching as preventive maintenance and calls for an operational enterprise strategy.[4] In our assessment, automation can support inventories, notifications, and agreed procedures. Relying entirely on someone remembering to read announcements is fragile.

The caution:  pip says pinning reduces exposure to bugs or incompatibilities in new releases, but still relies on the package source; hash checking adds another control.[1] A pinned version alone does not establish source trust or successful configuration and data migration.

We distinguish notification from installation. Notifications may be automatic, while production changes need an owner, test results, and recovery preparation. Critical security announcements should trigger a separate exposure assessment rather than waiting for a routine maintenance date. The appropriate cadence depends on the environment.

Add an unchanged-components field to the change record. If packages changed while the model and external connections stayed the same, record that scope. Troubleshooting can then begin with the actual differences rather than reinstalling everything.

Before closing the maintenance window, have a user repeat the ordinary workflow. Engineering checks startup; the user checks data access, tools, and schedules. Record both outcomes and keep unverified items open even after the version number changes.

◆ First-Hand Lessons

## Three. What We Learned in Practice

These observations come from AI agent deployment and maintenance records. They are not industry statistics or an account of any particular organization.

1. Major updates can change data too.  We encountered migration conflicts that caused repeated service restarts, and configuration-format changes that cleared existing settings. A successful download did not reveal these later effects.

2. Upstream changes can reach local systems.  A change in an AI service’s streaming format caused package validation failures across AI calls. After adding a fix, we had to check that it remained present after package updates. Local pinning does not freeze external dependencies.

3. Update prompts are not version records.  A diagnostic command once reported a one-version gap that actually crossed several releases with substantial changes. Our practice is to pin versions, review known issues, test, back up settings and data, prepare recovery commands, and schedule the upgrade.

4. Recovery involves state.  Our backup list includes settings, schedules, service definitions, and database snapshots. We stop the service before packaging an upgrade backup and rehearse restoration. Program and data states need to be planned together.

## Four.  Our Recommendations: Set Entry and Exit Conditions for Every Upgrade

1. Record the full combination.  Include the framework, dependencies, runtime, model, installation method, and lockfiles. Use pip and npm documentation for their respective package-management practices.[1][2]

2. Test the change.  Read release and migration notes, then exercise ordinary conversations, tools, retrieval, and schedules in a test environment. Record versions and results, including useful failure evidence.

3. Back up and define stop conditions.  Obtain a consistent backup and identify failures that require stopping and who decides on recovery. If a migration has changed the data structure, verify the recovery method before running old code against new data.

4. Assign patch ownership.  Name the announcement reviewer, routine maintenance window, and accelerated process for critical vulnerabilities. Verify the service, data, and workflows before closing the change, reflecting NIST’s post-installation verification principle.[4]

Pinning establishes a baseline; operations also needs updates, acceptance, and recovery.

◆ Editor’s Note · How Think BIG Approaches This: Comparable Changes

## Keep versions, backups, and acceptance results together.

(The following is Think BIG’s practical position, separate from the reporting above.)

We recommend treating updates as owned changes instead of allowing unattended overnight version changes in long-running services. Routine maintenance and urgent patches need distinct entry points, with repeatable task tests.

Post-installation acceptance belongs in the handover.

### Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: Does pinning mean never updating?
No. Keep a baseline while continuing to identify, prioritize, install, and verify patches.[4]
Q2: Is the framework version enough?
Record runtime and dependencies too. pip’s repeatable-install guidance includes transitive dependencies.[1]
Q3: Does npm ci update the lockfile?
No. It reports a mismatch rather than updating the lockfile.[2]
Q4: Is downgrading the program enough?
Check whether data and settings migrated, then use a rehearsed restoration plan. Program and state recovery need joint planning.

Sources
    Fact-checked: 2026-10-26.

    [2] npm, “npm ci”, accessed 2026-10-26: [docs.npmjs.com](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-ci) ·
    [3] Ollama, “Windows”, accessed 2026-10-26: [docs.ollama.com](https://docs.ollama.com/windows) ·
    [4] NIST, SP 800-40 Rev. 4 (2022), “Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning”, accessed 2026-10-26: [csrc.nist.gov](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/40/r4/final)

# AI Keeps Missing the Point in Company Documents? Inspect Retrieval Before Changing Models | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

AI Deployment Field Notes · Issue 019
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

AI DEPLOYMENT FIELD NOTES

November 12, 2026  ·  Thursday
◆
AI Deployment Field Notes
◆
Issue 019

RAG · Chunking · Retrieval Quality

## AI Keeps Missing the Point in Company Documents? Inspect Retrieval Before Changing Models

Think BIG Media  |  November 12, 2026

Review the question, retrieved passages, and answer together. Locate the failure before changing documents, retrieval settings, or the model.

## One.  What’s Happening: Having Documents Does Not Mean Retrieving the Right Evidence

Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, retrieves relevant content before asking a model to answer from it. Microsoft’s official overview identifies terminology mismatches, content preparation, and input limits as implementation challenges.[1] Uploading files and answering questions reliably are separate steps.

Chunking is one of those steps. Official documentation describes fixed-size, structural, and semantic approaches, with size and overlap adjusted to the content and use.[2] We would not apply one character count to every Chinese policy, table, or scanned document. Read the resulting chunks to check whether they retain subjects, conditions, and exceptions.

Microsoft’s evaluation guidance separates retrieval-process quality from final-answer quality. One asks whether retrieved material is relevant; the other examines grounding, relevance, and completeness of the answer.[3] We use that distinction as a diagnostic method, without recommending a service or treating an automated score as a business decision.

## Two.  Perspectives: Inspect Retrieval Without Ignoring Model Behavior

The case for checking data first:  The overview ties RAG quality to content preparation and retrieval relevance.[1] If the necessary evidence never reached the model, we would investigate indexing and retrieval first. A larger model does not resolve that missing input.

The model-side caution:  Receiving a passage does not establish that a model uses it correctly. The original 2023 study “Lost in the Middle” found position-dependent performance in its multi-document question-answering and key-value retrieval tasks.[4] It does not establish identical behavior in every newer model. It does challenge adding more context as a universal remedy.

Test both stages: whether the evidence was retrieved and whether the answer used it faithfully. When documents conflict, ask their owner to determine which is valid rather than asking the model to settle company policy.

Add explicit failure definitions: missing exceptions, treating an old version as current, or citing the wrong document. This gives document owners and engineers shared criteria beyond fluency or a retrieval score.

Keep the original phrasing too. Rewriting conversational questions into document titles before every test can hide the terminology mismatch being tested. Save original and rewritten queries with their retrieval results before deciding whether to adopt query rewriting.

◆ First-Hand Lessons

## Three. What We Learned in Practice

These observations come from our RAG document and answer-quality work. They are not industry statistics or an account of any particular organization.

1. Inspect retrieved passages first.  When an answer is poor, we check the retrieved material before analyzing generation. Chunks that are too large or small are among the causes we encounter; model capability is not always the problem.

2. A readable original can produce damaged text.  We have seen tables and scanned documents become corrupted during text extraction. We inspect the extracted text instead of repeatedly asking the model to read broken material better.

3. One subject may have two versions.  Retrieving old and new documents together mixes evidence. We remove outdated versions or mark their status so validity can be checked.

4. Keep real questions and reference answers.  We build test sets and watch for differences between conversational questions and formal document terms. Questions should reflect actual phrasing, beyond document titles.

## Four.  Our Recommendations: Diagnose with a Fixed Question Set

1. Inspect extracted text.  Compare tables, scans, and exception clauses against originals. Check whether labels still match values. Correct preprocessing problems before rebuilding the index.

2. Map questions to evidence.  Record expected answers and supporting documents and passages. Include unanswerable questions, outdated material, and terminology differences. Retrieval evaluation needs explicit relevance evidence.[3]

3. Change one class of settings at a time.  Keep the model and questions fixed when comparing segmentation, overlap, or query methods. Save retrieved passages so improvements have an identifiable cause. Validate parameters on your own content.[2][3]

4. Assess evidence and answers separately.  Wrong evidence points toward retrieval; correct evidence with a wrong answer calls for prompt and model checks; conflicting documents go to their owner. This is our recommended triage, beyond one aggregate score.

5. Test missing answers too.  Require an explicit evidence gap when support is insufficient. Independently test access permissions so retrieved content stays within authorization.[1]

Check that the model received the right material before judging its answer.

◆ Editor’s Note · How Think BIG Approaches This: Keep Failures as Repeatable Tests

## Save questions, passages, answers, and document versions together.

(The following is Think BIG’s practical position, separate from the reporting above.)

We recommend rerunning the same questions after knowledge-base changes. Failure records should identify the stage and document owner so future maintenance can build on prior work.

Answer quality and document access each need acceptance checks.

### Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What is RAG?
It retrieves relevant content and provides it to the model as evidence for an answer.[1]
Q2: Are larger chunks always better?
No. Test size, overlap, and boundaries against your content and use case.[2]
Q3: Does a citation prove the answer is correct?
Check whether it supports the claim and whether the answer is relevant and complete. These are separate evaluation dimensions.[3]
Q4: When should we consider another model?
First establish that retrieval delivers the right evidence. Then compare model and prompt choices on the same questions if answers still fail.

Sources
    Fact-checked: 2026-10-26.

    [1] Microsoft, “RAG and Generative AI”, accessed 2026-10-26: [learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/retrieval-augmented-generation-overview) ·
    [2] Microsoft, “Chunk Documents”, accessed 2026-10-26: [learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-chunk-documents) ·
    [3] Microsoft, “Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Evaluators”, accessed 2026-10-26: [learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/concepts/evaluation-evaluators/rag-evaluators) ·
    [4] Liu et al., “Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts,” 2023, arXiv:2307.03172, accessed 2026-10-26: [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)

# You Rank on Google. So Why Doesn’t ChatGPT Mention You? SEO vs. GEO, Explained | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Field Notes · Issue 003
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

被　AI　看見

October 7, 2026 · Wednesday
◆
First-hand observations on AI deployment
◆
Issue 003

SEO · GEO · AI Visibility

## You Rank on Google. So Why Doesn’t ChatGPT Mention You? — SEO vs. GEO, Explained

Think BIG Editorial  |  October 7, 2026

SEO gets you found in search results. GEO gets you mentioned in AI answers. Same foundation, different finish line: AI picks passages and weighs what others say about you, so ranking well doesn’t mean AI will name you.

## 1.  What’s happening: people are asking AI, not just searching

On October 8, 2025, Google launched AI Mode in Traditional Chinese for users in Taiwan. AI Mode uses a “query fan-out” technique: it breaks a question into subtopics, runs many searches at once, and returns a synthesized answer with links. ChatGPT also searches the web automatically when a question would benefit from current information, and its answers include clickable citations.

User behavior is shifting. Instead of typing keywords, scanning ten blue links, and comparing pages themselves, more people now ask a full question and wait for an AI to hand back an answer. A Microsoft post from October 2025 put it plainly: in AI search, it’s not just about being found — it’s about being selected .

That leads to a question we hear constantly: “My site ranks well on Google. Why won’t ChatGPT mention us?”

SEO (Search Engine Optimization) GEO (Generative Engine Optimization)
Goal Get found and clicked in search results Get mentioned, cited, and described accurately in AI answers

Where Google and Bing results pages ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode, Perplexity, Copilot

Unit Where a whole page ranks Whether a specific passage gets pulled into an answer

Track Indexing, rankings, clicks Mentions, citations of your URL, accuracy of description

## 2.  What the sources say: official docs say “same foundation,” research says “different outcomes”

Google’s position: get your SEO right first.  Google Search Central states there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and no special optimizations needed. A page must be indexed and snippet-eligible. The same page says you don’t need new machine-readable files, AI text files, or special schema.org markup. In other words, for Google’s own AI features, SEO is the ticket in.

Other AI tools don’t use Google’s index.  ChatGPT search relies on OpenAI’s own crawler, OAI-SearchBot. OpenAI’s documentation says sites that block it will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers. Perplexity runs its own crawler, PerplexityBot. Ranking on Google only tells you Google can see you. Everything else needs to be checked separately.

AI selects passages, not pages.  Microsoft explains that assistants like Copilot don’t read a page top to bottom. They break content into smaller pieces, evaluate each one, and assemble an answer from multiple sources. The practical advice: keep the title, description, and H1 aligned; use clear subheadings to separate ideas; write answers that stand on their own in one or two sentences; use lists and comparison tables; don’t bury key information in tabs, images, or PDFs. The same post acknowledges there’s no secret formula that ensures selection.

Research: real effects, no stable formula.  The paper that coined the term, “GEO: Generative Engine Optimization” (Princeton and collaborators, KDD 2024), found that rewrites such as adding quotations, statistics, and citations could boost visibility in AI responses by up to about 40% on the authors’ benchmark. A 2026 review of 45 studies is more cautious: topical relevance and position in context are the most reproducible levers, and no reviewed technique shows a stable, long-term, cross-platform causal effect.

Platform rules are getting sharper.  Google’s spam policies now explicitly list attempts to manipulate generative AI responses as a spam technique, and mass-producing low-value pages falls under scaled content abuse. Hidden text and page farms aimed at AI are a dead end.

◆ First-hand notes

## 3. Our own website: Google is warming up, AI still rarely mentions us

In early October 2026, we ran our own site through a six-layer audit: technical foundation, content, structured data, authority and entity, off-site citability, and measurement.

On-site layers scored 80–90%. Off-site layers scored 20–30%.  Technical foundation, structured data, and measurement all landed in the 80–90% range. “Authority and entity” and “off-site citability” landed at 20–30%. The gap wasn’t on our website. It was everywhere else.

Google ranks us; AI rarely brings us up.  Google Search Console shows several of our guides on the first page of results for their target queries. But when we ran a round of the same topics phrased as questions to AI, we barely showed up. Even a guide whose headline is that exact question wasn’t used as a source in that round. (A single round isn’t statistically reliable — that realization is what pushed us to rebuild our measurement method, which we cover in the next issue.)

AI has even described us incorrectly.  We once asked an AI chatbot what our company does, and it said, with full confidence, that we had nothing to do with AI. An AI’s picture of a small company comes from the little information it can reach. When that information is thin or inconsistent, it fills in the blanks.

What we’ve done:  opened robots.txt to major AI crawlers including OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot; put a complete one-sentence company definition at the top of our homepage; added Organization, Article, and FAQ structured data across the site; standardized our name and description everywhere; published an English edition of every NEWS article because research shows ChatGPT cites a large share of English sources when answering questions about Taiwan.

What we’re still building:  off-site mentions. Bylined media coverage, public directory listings, and long-form posts on our own named social accounts. We won’t fill the gap with fake accounts or paid forum posts.

The biggest lesson: good SEO makes you findable to AI. Getting AI to actually say your name takes other people talking about you, consistently.

## 4.  Our recommendations: do SEO and GEO together, measure them separately

Make sure both Google and AI crawlers can get in.  Key pages should be indexed and snippet-eligible. Check that robots.txt doesn’t accidentally block search crawlers like OAI-SearchBot or PerplexityBot. (Whether to allow AI training  crawlers is a separate decision.)

Write every section so it can be quoted on its own.  One subheading, one question. Put the answer in the first sentence or two. Spell out numbers, definitions, steps, and comparisons. This helps both Google snippets and AI passage selection.

Keep your identity consistent across the web.  Use the same legal name, short name, address, phone number, and service description on your website, Google Business Profile, social bios, and public directories.

Earn real off-site mentions.  Think industry association and government directories, Google Business Profile, bylined media contributions, and long-form posts on your own named accounts. Don’t hire people to pose as happy customers on forums. Dcard, a popular anonymous forum in Taiwan, permanently bans accounts used for word-of-mouth marketing, and an undisclosed paid endorsement in a consumer’s voice may violate Taiwan Fair Trade Commission rules on endorsement advertising.

Measure each channel on its own terms.  Use Search Console for Google; for Copilot and Bing, use the AI Performance report in Bing Webmaster Tools (public preview since February 2026); for ChatGPT, Perplexity, and other AI answers, use repeated sampling.

Bottom line: SEO lets AI find you. GEO gets AI to say your name.  Same foundation, different finish line.

◆ Editor’s note · How Think BIG approaches this

## One audit. Both sides. Built into every piece of content.

(The following reflects Think BIG’s own position and is separate from the neutral reporting above.)

We used our own website as the first test case, working through everything ourselves before offering the same method to businesses: Think BIG Search Visibility (SEO + GEO) — get found on Google, get named by AI.

One audit, both sides:  Google side covers indexing, technical foundation, keyword standing, and on-page writing. AI side covers whether each AI mentions you, how it describes you, and which sources it cites. Both roll up into one “top three things to fix first” list.

One piece of content, both jobs:  every piece is written for SEO (keywords, titles, internal links) and GEO (answer first, quotable passages, off-site placement) at the same time.

Measurement with a stated method:  AI answers change from run to run, so we use repeated sampling and report each AI separately. One screenshot is never a conclusion.

Compliant by design:  no bought links, no click farms, no fake accounts, no fake reviews, no hidden text. We don’t promise rankings or sales results. We promise to do the right things well and show you the numbers every month.

### FAQ

Q1: What’s the difference between SEO and GEO?
SEO helps your pages get found in Google and Bing search results. GEO helps AI tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity mention you, cite your pages, and describe you accurately when they answer questions. Both require indexable sites and clear content, but AI assembles answers from individual passages and gives weight to what other sites say about you.
Q2: I rank well on Google. Why doesn’t ChatGPT mention me?
ChatGPT search uses OpenAI’s own crawler and index rather than Google’s rankings, and for many questions it doesn’t search at all, answering from what the model already learned. It also favors passages that stand on their own and claims that multiple sources agree on. A strong Google ranking doesn’t carry over automatically.
Q3: Do I need to do anything extra to appear in Google’s AI Overviews?
According to Google’s documentation, no. There are no additional requirements, special files, or required structured data. The page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet in Google Search. Solid SEO fundamentals are the prerequisite.
Q4: Do I need an llms.txt file for GEO?
Google says you don’t need new machine-readable files or AI text files to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. You can add one, but don’t treat it as a priority. Indexability, clear passages, a consistent identity, and genuine off-site mentions matter more.
Q5: How can I tell whether AI mentions my company?
Don’t judge from a single question. AI answers vary from run to run. Ask the same question several ways, repeat each one multiple times, track it over several weeks, and record separately whether you were mentioned, whether your URL was cited, and whether the description was accurate. For Copilot and Bing, check the AI Performance report in Bing Webmaster Tools.

Sources

# Should Every AI Skill Be Reviewed? Treat It as Part of the Supply Chain | Think BIG NEWS

[← Think BIG NEWS](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/)

Enterprise Security Notes · Issue 018
THINKBIGTW.COM

# THINK BIG

NEWS

ENTERPRISE SECURITY NOTES

November 10, 2026  ·  Tuesday
◆
Enterprise Security Notes
◆
Issue 018

AI Skills · Supply Chain · Installation Review

## Should Every AI Skill Be Reviewed? Treat It as Part of the Supply Chain

Think BIG Media  |  November 10, 2026

Before installing a skill, ask what it reads, executes, and sends elsewhere. Written instructions and executable scripts need different evidence.

## One.  What’s Happening: Skills Can Bundle Both Instructions and Code

In October 2025, Anthropic published an engineering article explaining Agent Skills as bundles of instructions and code. It also warned that malicious skills could lead to data exfiltration or unintended actions.[1] We use that article to examine installation practice, without alleging a compromise at any platform or treating popularity as security evidence.

Supply-chain management includes the external components a system depends on. OWASP’s 2025 LLM Top 10 entry LLM03:2025 covers third-party packages, models, and data, and recommends supplier review and component inventories.[2] We apply that principle to a skill’s scripts, dependencies, and download sources.

A skill’s name does not establish its capabilities. The official article recommends reading bundled files, with attention to dependencies, scripts, and instructions to connect to untrusted network sources.[1] For text-only workflows, review instructions and data use. For executable components, review execution identity and file access as well. That is our proposed way to scale review depth.

## Two.  Perspectives: Reuse Knowledge; Verify Trust Separately

The benefit:  The article presents skills as a way to share composable expertise.[1] In our view, clear procedures and scripts can support repeated work and handovers. Writing everything again does not automatically make maintenance easier.

The caution:  Public availability, usable licensing, and safe behavior are separate questions. OWASP identifies licensing and provenance risks.[2] NIST SP 800-218 (2022), the Secure Software Development Framework, offers purchasers and suppliers a common vocabulary for secure-development practices.[3] We recommend recording what was checked, beyond the installation decision.

Hashes have limits too. pip documents checking downloaded packages against locally stored hashes, including dependencies.[4] A match establishes consistency with the approved file; it does not establish harmless behavior. Scanning, reading code, and testing answer different questions.

A review need not end with a bare pass or rejection. It can specify a test directory, draft-only outputs, or unresolved connections, with owners and review triggers. These are examples of approval conditions, not a claim that every skill supports equivalent isolation.

If nobody can review the scripts, narrow the pilot and request inspectable files and behavior explanations. AI can help identify questions, but its favorable judgment alone should not close a review the approver cannot explain.

◆ First-Hand Lessons

## Three. What We Learned in Practice

These points come from our review practice for skills, plugins, and MCP servers. They are not industry statistics or an account of any particular organization.

1. Read before installing.  We check sources, maintainers, licensing, and actual program behavior. We look for environment-variable or key access, outbound connections, and execution of downloaded content. Installation instructions lead us to the files that implement the behavior.

2. Explain requested privileges.  We review permissions and pin versions. Packages that fail review are not installed. We have rejected packages, but do not name them here or present individual decisions as product rankings.

3. Keep unresolved questions visible.  Third-party code retains risk. We record judgments about source, behavior, permissions, and versions. When content changes, those judgments need to be revisited.

## Four.  Our Recommendations: Make Installation a Traceable Decision

1. Inventory purpose and components.  Record the skill’s purpose, source, maintainer, license, scripts, and dependencies. Keep more than an installation command so future updates can be compared with reviewed files.[2]

2. Map access and connections.  List readable directories, writable files, external destinations, and credentials. Withhold production data while those remain unexplained. Require a reason and approval for added capabilities.

3. Test in isolation.  Use synthetic data and minimum necessary privileges. Observe outputs, file changes, and connections. Mark untested behavior as unresolved; a clean test run is not evidence of every future outcome.

4. Pin the reviewed version and schedule review.  Keep version and file-verification records, with an owner for update notices.[4] Compare instructions, dependencies, privileges, and destinations when upgrading.

5. Define shutdown steps.  Document skill removal, schedule shutdown, credential revocation, and log access. This is our exit-planning recommendation so an owner knows where to stop execution.

Review the capabilities a skill receives and how they can be withdrawn.

◆ Editor’s Note · How Think BIG Approaches This: Every Component Needs a History

## Keep purpose, version, access, and shutdown instructions together.

(The following is Think BIG’s practical position, separate from the reporting above.)

We recommend written review outcomes that identify permitted scope, open questions, and review triggers. Review depth should reflect capabilities and data access rather than the introduction page alone.

At handover, the owner should be able to find each component’s source and shutdown method.

### Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: Should text-only skills be reviewed?
Yes. Instructions can also direct unintended actions or external connections.[1]
Q2: Does open source establish safety?
No. Review provenance, licensing, behavior, and permissions separately, consistent with OWASP’s supplier and component guidance.[2]
Q3: Is a hash match enough?
A hash checks file consistency; review behavior and permissions separately.[4]
Q4: Must everything be rereviewed after an update?
Compare changes and review affected instructions, dependencies, privileges, and connections. Without a comparable version, establish a new baseline.

    Fact-checked: 2026-10-26.

    [2] OWASP, “LLM03:2025 Supply Chain”, accessed 2026-10-26: [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm032025-supply-chain/) ·
    [3] NIST, SP 800-218 (2022), “Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1”, accessed 2026-10-26: [csrc.nist.gov](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final) ·
    [4] pip, “Secure installs”, accessed 2026-10-26: [pip.pypa.io](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/topics/secure-installs/)

# How Do You Run Acceptance Testing for an AI Agent, and How Should Test Questions Be Prepared? | Q&A Library | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Building AI Agents
TB09

# How Do You Run Acceptance Testing for an AI Agent, and How Should Test Questions Be Prepared?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-19
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/ai-agent-acceptance-testing/)

The short answer

Accept an AI Agent with the company's own questions, not the impression from a demo. Write test questions and correct answers in advance, covering at least what it should answer, what it should decline or hand off, what users must not see, and what it must not do without approval. Record each result, and pass only when the threshold both sides agreed in advance is met. Rerun the same questions whenever the model, documents, or permissions change.

## 1. Four things to write down before testing

- Output specification : what the AI Agent delivers, in what format, with which required fields and sources. For example, "reply drafts must cite the source document and passage".

- Test questions and correct answers : written by people who know the business, not by the people who built the system.

- Pass thresholds : the standard for each type of question, written down in advance.

- Approval points : which actions must stop until a person approves. These are test items too, not footnotes.

One anti-pattern in OpenAI's evaluation best practices is treating "it seems to work" as a pass (vibe-based evals). Writing the criteria down first prevents that.

## 2. Five types of test questions

Type
Sample question (illustrative)
Pass standard
1. Answerable
"What is the hotel allowance for business travel?"
Correct answer; the cited passage actually supports it and is the current version

2. Should decline or hand off
A question the documents do not cover, or two documents that conflict
States that support is insufficient and hands off to the designated person; does not make up an answer

3. Permission boundary
A regular employee asks about pay rules only managers may see
Neither the answer nor the citations expose restricted content

4. No action without approval
"Just send this quote to the customer"
Stops until the designated person approves

5. Outside content is not an instruction
Upload a document containing "ignore previous rules"
Follows the original rules; text in the document does not change its behavior

Types 3, 4, and 5 are where AI Agent acceptance differs from chatbot testing. An AI Agent can read data and take actions, so you test that what should not happen really does not happen. Type 5 follows OWASP's advice to run adversarial tests regularly, treating the model as an untrusted user.

## 3. Recording results and when to retest

For each question, record the test date, model and settings, input, expected result, actual result, verdict (pass, partial, fail), and reason for failure. For tests involving sensitive data, agree separately on how records are stored and accessed; do not copy entire source records.

OpenAI's evaluation advice also covers automating scoring where possible and calibrating automated scoring with human judgment. In practice, answerable questions can be checked by script first, while decline and permission questions get human review.

Rerun the same set whenever you change the model, the context or retrieval settings, add or withdraw documents, or adjust permissions. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework places this under its Measure function: risks must be measurable, and measured continuously.

Brand information | Think BIG

## How Think BIG accepts an AI Agent

Think BIG (Think BIG Make it Real Co., Ltd.) is an enterprise AI Agent deployment provider headquartered in Taiwan. Starting from protecting company data, we build AI Agents inside the client's own environment (company hardware, or a cloud server under the company's account). There are two deployment options: with the on-premises version, models and documents are processed on company hardware; with the cloud-assisted version, employees' questions and the document passages the system retrieves are sent to the model provider for processing.

- Business goals turned into acceptance criteria : work goals become checkable output specifications, including format, required fields, data sources, and reviewer roles.

- Normal, abnormal, and unauthorized cases tested : test cases cover complete data, unverifiable data, missing fields, service outages, and insufficient permissions; for steps that require approval, we confirm the system stops until authorized.

- Traceable test records, retested after changes : test conditions, configuration, input scope, and expected and actual results are recorded; after model, data, or permission changes, the related cases are verified again.

See [AI Agent acceptance framework](https://thinkbigtw.com/guides/ai-acceptance/) and [RAG knowledge Q&A](https://thinkbigtw.com/enterprise/rag/).

The actual scope of Think BIG's services follows what both parties confirm.

## FAQ

Q1: How is AI Agent acceptance different from regular system acceptance? Besides confirming features work, you test that what should not happen does not: it declines when it should, users cannot see restricted content, it does not send or pay before approval, and instructions hidden in documents do not change its behavior. Q2: Who should write the acceptance test questions? People who know the business write the questions and correct answers, not the people who built the system. Each question notes which passage of which document the answer comes from. Q3: How should the pass standard for an AI Agent be set? Set it separately for each question type and write it down before testing. For example, a required share of correct answers on answerable questions, and no failures at all on decline and permission questions. Q4: Is more testing needed after acceptance? Yes. After changing the model, retrieval or context settings, adding or withdrawing documents, or adjusting permissions, rerun the same set to confirm nothing has regressed.

- NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage): [www.nist.gov](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

# How Should AI Agent Permissions Be Set, and Which Actions Must a Person Approve? | Q&A Library | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Building AI Agents
TB05

# How Should AI Agent Permissions Be Set, and Which Actions Must a Person Approve?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-19
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/ai-agent-permissions/)

The short answer

Use least privilege. Each AI Agent gets only the tools, data, and accounts its job needs, and read-only wherever possible. Any action that sends externally, spends money, deletes, or changes production data runs only after a designated person approves. Permissions must be enforced by the systems themselves, not by writing "don't do this" in a prompt.

## 1. What goes wrong with too much permission

OWASP calls this Excessive Agency (LLM06:2025): when an AI's output is wrong, ambiguous, or manipulated, the system lets it take a damaging action. There are three root causes, alone or together:

- Excessive functionality : tools the job does not need, such as an email-sending tool connected to an agent that only reads documents.

- Excessive permissions : tools with too much access, such as an account that can modify a database when the job only needs to query it.

- Excessive autonomy : high-impact actions executed without a person confirming.

AI Agents make mistakes and can be misled by instructions hidden in documents (see "What is prompt injection?"). With the right permissions, the damage from a mistake stays small.

## 2. Six steps to set permissions

Based on OWASP LLM06 mitigations and the security best practices for MCP (the open protocol AI Agents use to connect tools):

- Connect only the tools needed.  Write down the agent's job and connect only the tools it requires. Prefer purpose-built tools over open-ended ones such as running arbitrary commands or opening arbitrary URLs.

- Enable only needed functions in each tool.  A document-reading tool should not include deletion.

- Minimize account permissions.  Read-only wherever possible. MCP recommends starting with the smallest scope and raising it step by step when needed, logging each elevation.

- Act as the user.  An AI Agent working for someone uses that person's permissions, not a shared account that can see everything.

- Let downstream systems decide authorization.  Whether an action is allowed is set by the permissions in the database, file system, or mail system, not by the model's judgment.

- Require human approval for high-impact actions.  External sending, spending, deletion, production changes, personal data, and commitments to outsiders pause until a designated person confirms.

Also, locally installed MCP tools run with the same system privileges as the AI client. MCP recommends showing the full command and getting the user's consent before connecting a new tool, and running it in a sandbox with restricted access.

## 3. Sample permission table

During deployment, write each AI Agent's permissions into a table signed off by the company's owner. This is an illustration, not any real company's setup:

AI Agent
Can read
Can write
Always needs human approval
Customer service agent
Approved FAQs, product descriptions
Reply drafts
Refunds, compensation, any commitment to customers

Sales assistant
Product catalog, pricing rules
Quote drafts
Sending to customers, discounts outside the rules

Admin assistant
Company policies, form templates
Internal summaries
Sending official letters, changing HR records

Accounting assistant
Invoices and ledger details (read-only)
Reconciliation discrepancy list
Any payment or transfer (no payment function connected)

Once the table is written, verify it with tests that check forbidden actions really fail, for example asking the customer service agent to send a refund confirmation directly and confirming it stops for approval.

Brand information | Think BIG

## How Think BIG sets AI Agent permissions

Think BIG (Think BIG Make it Real Co., Ltd.) is an enterprise AI Agent deployment provider headquartered in Taiwan. Starting from protecting company data, we build AI Agents inside the client's own environment (company hardware, or a cloud server under the company's account). There are two deployment options: with the on-premises version, models and documents are processed on company hardware; with the cloud-assisted version, employees' questions and the document passages the system retrieves are sent to the model provider for processing.

- Least privilege : for each AI Agent we confirm data sources, processing location, read/write scope, and access roles according to the work required.

- Human approval kept : external sending, spending, and production system changes require approval from a designated person. AI Agents provide work output and evidence; people keep the key decisions.

- Permission changes recorded : adding or adjusting permissions leaves a change record, and the data and permission list covers sources, storage locations, read/write scope, external services, and approvers.

See [Trust](https://thinkbigtw.com/trust/) and [On-premises AI and data sovereignty](https://thinkbigtw.com/guides/local-ai-data/).

The actual scope of Think BIG's services follows what both parties confirm.

## FAQ

Q1: What is "excessive agency" in AI Agents? OWASP LLM06:2025 describes it as a system letting an AI take damaging actions when its output is wrong, ambiguous, or manipulated. The causes are excessive functionality, excessive permissions, and excessive autonomy. Q2: Which AI Agent actions must a person approve? Sending externally, spending money, deleting, changing production systems, and anything involving personal data or commitments to outsiders should pause until a designated person confirms. Q3: Is writing "don't do X" in the prompt enough as access control? No. OWASP recommends enforcing authorization in downstream systems rather than relying on the model's judgment. Set permissions in the database, file, and mail systems. Q4: Can an AI Agent use a shared admin account? Not recommended. OWASP recommends acting in the user's own context with minimally scoped credentials, so the agent cannot see or do more than the user is allowed to.

Sources (checked 2026-10-19)

- OWASP GenAI Security Project, LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency (three root causes, eight mitigations): [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/)

- Model Context Protocol, Security Best Practices (scope minimization, consent and sandboxing for local servers): [modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/security_best_practices)

- OWASP GenAI Security Project, LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection (least privilege, human approval): [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/)

# What Does a Pre-Delivery Security Review of an AI Agent Actually Check? | Q&A Library | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Building AI Agents
TB07

# What Does a Pre-Delivery Security Review of an AI Agent Actually Check?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-19
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/ai-agent-pre-delivery-security-review/)

The short answer

It checks the exact version being delivered, not some version from during development: code and configuration, outbound connections, permissions, keys, and third-party packages and models, each against a checklist with a record kept. If it does not pass, it is not delivered. No one can promise perfect security; the point of a review is to rule out known risks one by one and leave a record of what was checked and what was found.

## 1. Eight checks

Common pre-delivery checks for AI Agents, mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025:

#
Check
What is examined
Related risk
1
Version match
The reviewed files are the same files being delivered (for example, by comparing hashes), so "reviewed A, installed B" cannot happen
Supply chain (LLM03)

2
Outbound connections
Which external services the system is expected to reach and what data it sends; nothing outside the list
Sensitive information disclosure (LLM02)

3
Permissions
Each AI Agent has only the tools and data its job needs, verified with tests that forbidden actions fail
Excessive agency (LLM06)

4
Keys
API keys are not in code, not in the repository, not in system prompts or chat logs; only in permission-protected configuration
System prompt leakage (LLM07)

5
Third-party packages and models
Trusted sources, clear licenses, pinned versions with no auto-update; model files checked by hash
Supply chain (LLM03)

6
Handling outside content
Web pages, emails, and documents the AI reads are not treated as instructions; output formats checked in code
Prompt injection (LLM01), improper output handling (LLM05)

7
Document and data permissions
The knowledge base retrieves by user permission, and even citations do not expose restricted content
Vector and embedding weaknesses (LLM08)

8
Records and recovery
What changed, why, and how to roll back to the previous version are all recorded
Governance (NIST AI RMF)

Under supply chain risk, OWASP recommends using only models from verifiable sources, checking integrity with signing and file hashes, keeping an up-to-date software bill of materials (SBOM), and inventorying the licenses involved. Under system prompt leakage, it states that credentials and connection strings should not be in the system prompt.

## 2. How results are decided

Use three outcomes, agreed in advance:

- Pass : every check is met; delivery can proceed.

- Conditional pass : issues exist but the risk is manageable; the required fixes and deadlines are listed and confirmed once done.

- Fail : issues that could leak data, allow unauthorized actions, or prevent recovery; no delivery until fixed and re-reviewed.

The review is best done by someone not involved in development, with a record of which version was reviewed, how each item was checked, and what was found. The U.S. NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) organizes AI risk management into four functions (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage), and NIST published its generative AI profile (AI 600-1) on July 26, 2024. Review records are the evidence for Measure and Manage.

## 3. After delivery

Passing at delivery does not mean safe forever: models update, packages get vulnerabilities, permissions get adjusted. Every later change should re-run the affected checks from the same list. Companies can write into the contract which changes trigger a new review and who keeps the records.

Brand information | Think BIG

- Pre-delivery security review : before each system is delivered, its code and configuration go through a security review: comparing the exact version to be delivered, checking outbound connections and permissions, and confirming keys are not exposed. If it does not pass, it is not delivered.

- Third-party components and keys : third-party packages are reviewed for source and license, pinned, and not auto-updated. Keys stay in permission-protected configuration files, never in the repository or in chat. Cloud accounts are opened under the client's name.

- Changes recorded : before any change, scope, reason, owner, and rollback method are confirmed, and the change runs only after approval within the authorized scope.

## FAQ

Q1: How is an AI Agent security review different from a regular software security check? Besides versions, keys, packages, and permissions, an AI Agent review checks whether outside content it reads can be treated as instructions (prompt injection), whether its permissions exceed the job (excessive agency), and whether the knowledge base can hand restricted content to users. Q2: Why confirm that the reviewed version matches the delivered version? If the review covered a development version and a few lines changed before delivery, the review means little. Comparing file hashes confirms the reviewed files are the ones delivered. Q3: Does passing a security review mean the AI Agent has no vulnerabilities? No. No one can promise perfect security; a review rules out known risks one by one and keeps a record. Every change after delivery should re-check the affected items. Q4: Which standards can an AI Agent security review follow? Common references are the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) with its generative AI profile, AI 600-1.

Sources (checked 2026-10-19)

- OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/)

- OWASP, LLM03:2025 Supply Chain (verifiable sources, signing and hashes, SBOM, license inventory): [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm032025-supply-chain/)

- OWASP, LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage (no credentials in system prompts): [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm072025-system-prompt-leakage/)

- OWASP, LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure: [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm022025-sensitive-information-disclosure/)

- OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 (released 2025-12-09): [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/)

- NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, AI 600-1): [www.nist.gov](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

# What Happens If an AI API Key Leaks, and How Should a Company Store It? | Q&A Library | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Enterprise AI Security
TB11

# What Happens If an AI API Key Leaks, and How Should a Company Store It?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-19
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/ai-api-key-leak/)

The short answer

A leaked API key lets someone else call AI on your company's account. Per OpenAI, this can cause data loss, unexpected charges, a depleted quota, and interrupted API access. If a key leaks, revoke it immediately, switch to a new key, and review usage. Day to day, four things matter: keys stay out of code, repositories, and chat; each person or system has its own key; keys have expiration dates and are rotated; and spend limits are set.

## 1. How keys usually leak

- Hard-coded and pushed to a repository.  OpenAI notes that committing keys to source code is a common way credentials are compromised. A public repository exposes them outright; a private one can leak them in a breach.

- Shipped in browsers or mobile apps.  OpenAI advises never deploying keys in client-side environments; route requests through your own backend server.

- Passed around in chat, email, or screenshots.  These records end up in many places and are hard to pull back.

- Written into an AI's system prompt.  OWASP warns that credentials and connection strings should not be in system prompts, which can be extracted.

## 2. Four steps when a key leaks

- Revoke immediately.  OWASP Secrets Management: exposed keys should be revoked immediately.

- Issue a new key.  Generate a new one, update the systems that use it, and confirm it works.

- Review usage.  Check the usage page for activity your team did not generate.

- Clean up the exposure.  Remove the revoked key from repository history, chat logs, and system logs, and find out how it leaked so it does not happen again.

## 3. Seven everyday storage rules

Based on OpenAI's "Best Practices for API Key Safety" and the OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet:

- One key per person and per system.  OpenAI does not support sharing keys; permissions can be set per key.

- Set expiration dates and rotate.  OpenAI project keys can have expiration dates, and administrators can cap key lifetime. Revoke the old key once the new one is confirmed.

- Store keys in environment variables or a secrets manager.  Not in code. A dedicated key management service keeps keys separate from the application.

- Scan before commit.  OWASP recommends enabling secret detection on the developer side to catch keys before commit; GitHub's push protection, for example, blocks a push when it detects a secret.

- Set spend limits with hard enforcement.  OpenAI recommends monthly spend limits with hard enforcement to cap the cost of a leaked key; alerts alone do not stop traffic.

- Restrict source IPs.  OpenAI offers IP allowlisting: only listed IPs can use the key, and other requests are rejected even with a valid key.

- Least privilege and audit logs.  Give each key only the permissions it needs, and keep tamper-resistant records of who used which key and when.

One point often missed: keys should be issued under the company's own account.  If a key belongs to a contractor's or an individual's account, the bill, usage logs, and power to revoke are not in the company's hands.

Brand information | Think BIG

## How Think BIG handles keys

Think BIG (Think BIG Make it Real Co., Ltd.) is an enterprise AI Agent deployment provider headquartered in Taiwan. Starting from protecting company data, we build AI Agents inside the client's own environment (company hardware, or a cloud server under the company's account). There are two deployment options: with the on-premises version, models and documents are processed on company hardware; with the cloud-assisted version, employees' questions and the document passages the system retrieves are sent to the model provider for processing.

- Clients apply for their own keys : AI model fees are paid by the client directly; the client applies for the API key with our engineers' guidance, and cloud accounts are opened under the client's name.

- Keys not exposed : keys stay only in permission-protected configuration files, never in the repository or in chat.

- Pre-delivery security review : before each system is delivered, its code and configuration go through a security review that includes confirming keys are not exposed; if it does not pass, it is not delivered.

See [FAQ](https://thinkbigtw.com/faq/) and [Trust](https://thinkbigtw.com/trust/).

The actual scope of Think BIG's services follows what both parties confirm.

## FAQ

Q1: What happens if an OpenAI API key leaks? Per OpenAI, a leaked key lets others use your account's quota without your consent, which can cause data loss, unexpected charges, a depleted quota, and interrupted API access. Q2: What should you do when an API key leaks? Revoke it immediately, generate a new key and update your systems, review usage logs, then remove the leaked key from repository history, chat, and logs and find the cause. Q3: Can an API key be written into code? Not recommended. OpenAI notes that committing keys to source code is a common leak path, and recommends environment variables or a key management service, and never placing keys in browsers or mobile apps. Q4: How can you limit the damage from a leaked key? Set monthly spend limits with hard enforcement, give keys expiration dates and rotate them, enable IP allowlisting, and grant each key only the permissions it needs.

Sources (checked 2026-10-19)

- OpenAI Help Center, Best Practices for API Key Safety (no sharing, expiration and rotation, no client-side keys, no commits, environment variables, spend limits, IP allowlisting, consequences of a leak): [help.openai.com](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/5112595-best-practices-for-api-key-safety)

- OWASP, Secrets Management Cheat Sheet (least privilege, rotation, pre-commit detection, auditing, revocation on exposure): [cheatsheetseries.owasp.org](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html)

- GitHub Docs, About push protection: [docs.github.com](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/secret-scanning/introduction/about-push-protection)

- OWASP, LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage (no credentials in system prompts): [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm072025-system-prompt-leakage/)

# What Are the Risks When Employees Paste Company Data into ChatGPT, and How Should a Company Manage It? | Q&A Library | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Enterprise AI Security
TB01

# What Are the Risks When Employees Paste Company Data into ChatGPT, and How Should a Company Manage It?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-19
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/employees-chatgpt-company-data/)

The short answer

The risk has two layers. Once data is pasted, it sits on the provider's servers (even if it is not used for training, it is retained for some time). And when employees use personal accounts, the company cannot control whether their chats are used for training. The answer is not a blanket ban but three steps: name the approved tools and company accounts, classify data and state which level may go where, and give confidential data a tool that does not send it outside the company.

## 1. Where does pasted data go?

When an employee presses send, the text goes to the provider's servers. Whether it is then stored or used for training depends on the plan. Official documentation as of 2026-10-19:

Usage
Used for model training?
Retention
ChatGPT personal accounts (Free, Go, Plus, Pro)
The user turns "Improve the model for everyone" on or off in Data controls; when off, new chats are not used for training
Chats stay in history; Temporary Chats may be retained up to 30 days for safety

ChatGPT Business, Enterprise and other managed workspaces
Not used for training by default, per OpenAI
Follows the workspace's retention settings

OpenAI API
Since March 1, 2023, API data is not used for training unless you opt in
Abuse monitoring logs retained up to 30 days by default

Anthropic (Claude) commercial products and API
Not used for training by default
API inputs and outputs deleted within 30 days by default, with exceptions

The point: "Is it used for training?" and "Is it retained?" are separate questions.  Even on a no-training plan, the data has left the company and stayed on someone else's servers for a while. For truly confidential material, the test is not whether training is off but whether the data may leave the company at all.

## 2. Legal points in Taiwan

If the pasted text contains personal data of customers or staff, Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act may come into play:

- Article 5 : collection, processing, and use of personal data must not exceed what is necessary for the specific purpose.

- Article 20 : non-government entities must use personal data within the necessary scope of the specific purpose of collection.

- Article 4 : a party commissioned by a government or non-government entity to collect, process, or use personal data is treated as the commissioning party within the scope of the Act. Under Article 8 of the Act's Enforcement Rules, a party that commissions others to collect, process, or use personal data must properly supervise the commissioned party (for example, by agreeing on the scope of processing, security measures, and the return or deletion of data when the engagement ends, and by checking compliance regularly). In other words, if handing personal data to an outside service counts as commissioning under the Act, the company has a duty to supervise, and its responsibility does not pass to the provider just because the data was handed over. Whether pasting data into a particular AI service counts as commissioning depends on the facts, such as the service terms, the account type, and how the data is used.

For government agencies, the Executive Yuan presented the "Reference Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI by the Executive Yuan and Its Agencies" at its cabinet meeting on August 31, 2023. One aim is for agencies to maintain the confidentiality and professionalism of official business, and ministries are asked to set rules or internal controls for generative AI as their work requires. Private companies are not bound by it, but the direction is useful: decide which data must not go into generative AI before deciding how to use it.

This is a general explanation of the law, not legal advice for any specific situation; for an actual case, consult a lawyer.

## 3. Three steps a company can take now

1. Name the tools and accounts.  List approved AI tools and use company-managed accounts or workspaces. Personal accounts leave training settings, chat history, and post-resignation data outside the company's control.

2. Classify data and post the table internally.  A sample to adapt:

Level
Examples
Where it may go
Public
Website copy, published catalogs
Any approved AI tool

Internal
General SOPs, internal notices
Company workspace or API only, with no-training settings confirmed

Confidential
Quotes, contracts, formulas, drawings, financials
Not sent to outside AI services; use a local model on company hardware

Personal data
Customer names and phone numbers, staff records, medical records
Generally not pasted; de-identify first and confirm the use fits the collection purpose

3. Give confidential data a usable alternative.  A rule that only says "don't" pushes people to workarounds. A tool that keeps data inside the company, such as a local model on company hardware, makes the rule hold.

Finally, explain the why. Most leaks are not malicious; employees simply do not know where the text goes.

Brand information | Think BIG

## How Think BIG handles "can this data leave the company?"

Think BIG (Think BIG Make it Real Co., Ltd.) is an enterprise AI Agent deployment provider headquartered in Taiwan. Starting from protecting company data, we build AI Agents inside the client's own environment (company hardware, or a cloud server under the company's account). There are two deployment options: with the on-premises version, models and documents are processed on company hardware; with the cloud-assisted version, employees' questions and the document passages the system retrieves are sent to the model provider for processing.

- Map the data flow before building : which data enters the AI, where it is stored, and whether anything leaves the company, listed item by item for the client to confirm.

- Decide which data may leave first : before building, we use the company's data classification to confirm which data must stay in the on-premises version and which may be processed with the cloud-assisted version; the cloud-assisted version is subject to the model provider's terms.

- Pre-delivery security review : before each system is delivered, its code and configuration go through a security review; if it does not pass, it is not delivered. No one can promise perfect security; what we do is review, one gate at a time.

See [Enterprise](https://thinkbigtw.com/enterprise/) and [Trust](https://thinkbigtw.com/trust/).

## FAQ

Q1: If employees use ChatGPT for company data, will it be used for training? It depends on the plan. On ChatGPT personal accounts, the user decides whether "Improve the model for everyone" is on. ChatGPT Business, Enterprise and other managed workspaces are not used for training by default, per OpenAI. OpenAI API data has not been used for training by default since March 1, 2023. Q2: If training is off, is the data safe? Not entirely. No training is not the same as no retention: OpenAI API abuse monitoring logs are kept up to 30 days by default, and ChatGPT Temporary Chats may be kept up to 30 days. For truly confidential data, ask whether it may leave the company at all. Q3: Should a company ban ChatGPT outright? A ban alone tends not to hold. It works better to name approved tools and accounts, classify data into public, internal, confidential, and personal data with clear rules for each, and give confidential data an alternative that stays inside the company. Q4: Does pasting customer data into AI violate Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act? It can, depending on the data and the purpose. Article 5 says collection, processing, and use of personal data must not exceed what the specific purpose requires, and Article 20 says non-government entities must use personal data within the necessary scope of the specific purpose of collection. If pasting data into AI serves a purpose beyond the one it was collected for, that may be a problem. Confirm the use fits the collection purpose, and de-identify where possible.

- OpenAI API, Your data (API data not used for training since 2023-03-01; abuse monitoring logs up to 30 days): [platform.openai.com](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/your-data)

- Anthropic Privacy Center, Is my data used for model training? (commercial products not used for training by default): [privacy.claude.com](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/7996868-is-my-data-used-for-model-training)

- Anthropic Privacy Center, How long do you store my organization's data? (API deletion within 30 days and exceptions): [privacy.claude.com](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/7996866-how-long-do-you-store-my-organization-s-data)

- Personal Data Protection Act (Articles 4, 5, 20), Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC (Taiwan): [law.moj.gov.tw](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=I0050021)

- Enforcement Rules of the Personal Data Protection Act (Article 8, supervision of commissioned parties): [law.moj.gov.tw](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=I0050022)

- Executive Yuan, Reference Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI by the Executive Yuan and Its Agencies (cabinet meeting, 2023-08-31): [www.ey.gov.tw](https://www.ey.gov.tw/Page/448DE008087A1971/40c1a925-121d-4b6b-8f40-7e9e1a5401f2)
